annex.description: Twenty-four methods across eras. Annex practice never changes the medieval journey or writes later traditions into its history.
annex.heading: Compendium of Methods · Annex
annex.journey_blocked: This method does not belong to the current era; it remains available in the methods annex.
annex.practice_complete: Annex practice complete; the journey state was not changed.
arch.battuta.name: A traveler in Battuta's manner
arch.battuta.obsession: Cross the sea roads; come to Mecca from every direction.
arch.cartographer.name: A maker of road maps
arch.cartographer.obsession: Keep hearsay directions separate from roads personally walked.
arch.healer.name: An itinerant healer
arch.healer.obsession: Trade remedies along the post roads, and record the limits of each cure.
arch.merchant.name: A merchant of the sea road
arch.merchant.obsession: Follow the monsoon; weave a net across the ocean.
arch.pilgrim.name: A pilgrim of the far road
arch.pilgrim.obsession: Travel through networks of scholars and hostels without treating unfamiliar rites as obstacles.
arch.polo.name: A traveller in Polo’s manner
arch.polo.obsession: Go east, and reach the Kaan’s court.
arch.scribe.name: A multilingual scribe
arch.scribe.obsession: Leave records that speakers of different languages can check against one another.
arch.steppe.name: The steppe road
arch.steppe.obsession: Cross the grass, and see the Kaan’s tents.
arch.translator.name: A translator of the trade roads
arch.translator.obsession: Let two accounts stand side by side before deciding which is true.
book.battuta.blurb: Battuta's voice opens the Islamic cities Polo scarcely names — Cairo, Mecca, Damascus, Delhi, the Maldives. Our bindings use passage-level extracts, not whole abridged chapters, so each city citation can be checked in one glance.
book.battuta.passage: I left Tangier, my birthplace, on Thursday the second of Rajab 725, with the intention of making the Pilgrimage to the Holy House and visiting the tomb of the Prophet. I swore that I would never travel a second time the same road, if I could help it — and for years the roads kept that oath for me.
book.battuta.subtitle: The Rihla · Tangier to the ends of the earth
book.battuta.title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta
book.conti.blurb: A Venetian merchant's years in Calicut, Pegu and Malabar, written down by Poggio after Conti's confession in Rome. Public-domain Major translation. Useful for the Indian Ocean desk and monsoon notes.
book.conti.passage: Calicut is a maritime city, noble and noted for its harbour. Pepper grows here in great abundance. Ships come from all parts of India, from Ethiopia, Arabia and China. Conti lived here long enough to learn the tongue of the merchants.
book.conti.subtitle: Hakluyt Society 1857 · India in the Fifteenth Century
book.conti.title: The Travels of Niccolò de' Conti
book.odoric.blurb: Odoric saw Zayton's harbour and the bridges of Cansay a generation after Polo. Yule's edition is public domain. Desk passages sit beside Polo's China without displacing his chapter bindings.
book.odoric.passage: I came to a certain city called Zayton, which hath a port twice as great as any in the world. In this city friars dwell, and porcelain is made in great quantity. From Zayton one may sail to many isles of India.
book.odoric.subtitle: Yule 1866 · Cathay and the Way Thither
book.odoric.title: The Travels of Friar Odoric
book.pinto.blurb: Fernão Mendes Pinto's sprawling romance of captivity and coasts. Our English excerpt is rough machine prose — honest enough for a desk leaf, never strong enough to bind a city. Marked authored / desk-only.
book.pinto.passage: I spent one-and-twenty years in the parts of India, Ethiopia, Arabia, China and the eastern archipelago — thirteen times a captive, seventeen times sold. I leave this rude writing so that my children may see the labours of that road.
book.pinto.subtitle: Desk excerpt · not used as city evidence
book.pinto.title: Peregrinação · Mendes Pinto
book.polo.blurb: The spine of this game's first chapter. Polo's book is cut into places and stories that feed city entries, road encounters, and the codex. What you read on the map can usually be traced back to a chapter here.
book.polo.passage: When you leave the city of Tauris (Tabriz) and ride east, you enter a land of many cities and of merchants who know every road from the Black Sea to Cathay. Of Cambaluc and of Kinsay the book speaks at length — of courts, of canals, of harbours thick with masts. This desk keeps only a leaf; the journey keeps the rest.
book.polo.subtitle: Yule–Cordier · Venice to Cathay
book.polo.title: The Travels of Marco Polo
book.rubruck.blurb: A Franciscan's report from 1253–55: felt idols, kumiss, and a debate before the Khan at Caracarum. Public-domain Rockhill translation. Excerpts feed the steppe desk and legend of the religious disputation.
book.rubruck.passage: Of the city of Caracarum you must know that, exclusive of the palace of the Khan, it is not as large as the village of Saint Denis. There are two quarters in it: one of the Saracens, where the market is; the other of the Cathayans, who are all craftsmen. There are twelve temples of idols, two mosques, and one Christian church at the far end of the town.
book.rubruck.subtitle: Rockhill 1900 · to the court of Mangu Khan
book.rubruck.title: The Journey of William of Rubruck
book.tafur.blurb: A Castilian gentleman's tour of 1435–39: Constantinople, Cairo, Cyprus. The Letts English version (1926) is public domain in the United States. Desk excerpts only — bindings stay conservative.
book.tafur.passage: I came to Constantinople, which is a great city, though much of it is in ruins. Saint Sophia still stands in majesty, and the walls that have held so many sieges yet enclose the city. Across the Horn the Genoese keep Pera.
book.tafur.subtitle: Letts 1926 · Mediterranean and the Near East
book.tafur.title: Travels and Adventures of Pero Tafur
book.zhenghe.blurb: Chinese harbour chapters for Champa, Java, Malacca, Calicut, Aden and Hormuz. The desk reads from the classical Chinese abridgement; English glosses are authored for play. City map bindings remain with Polo where he already speaks; Zheng He's voice lives here and in the maritime codex.
book.zhenghe.passage: 自闽之长乐县五虎门发舟，西南行顺风约十日可抵占城。港岸立石塔为标，舶至是系焉。王尚释教，跨象或乘小车。市交易以金，极宝爱中国青磁器暨纻丝。
book.zhenghe.subtitle: Ma Huan / Zhang Sheng · Zheng He's voyages
book.zhenghe.title: Yingya Shenglan · The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores

city.zayton.market.desc: The quay of Zayton runs the length of the water and is never quiet. Pepper comes ashore in sacks the height of a man; there are pearls weighed out in little brass scales, and lignaloes and sandalwood stacked like cordwood. You must know that the merchant pays dearly here: the Kaan takes a tamghā on everything, ten in the hundred, and the ship's charge on top of it — thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper. Between the freight and the Kaan's due a man pays out a good half of what his cargo is worth. And yet on the other half he makes so great a profit that he is always glad to come back with more.
city.zayton.market.name: The Quay at Zayton
city.zayton.name: Zayton
city.zayton.shrine.desc: Above the anchorage, on a hill that catches the first light off the sea, stands the temple of the sea-goddess. Her gilded image faces south over the water; at her feet lie the offerings of shipmasters — paper burnt, rice set out, a cup of wine. No master of this coast puts out without going up to her first, and none of them calls it fortune-telling. They call it asking.
city.zayton.shrine.name: The Temple of the Sea
city.zayton.wonder: You have heard men speak of Alexandria and her hundred spired warehouses. Know this: for every shipload of pepper that reaches Alexandria bound for Christendom, a hundred such come in to this haven of Zayton — aye, and more too. The ships of India crowd the water so thickly that their masts, seen from the hill at sunrise, look like a burnt forest. And it is not only pepper. Precious stones, pearls, spicery of every kind that grows, silk enough to clothe an empire — all of it passes through this quay, and the Kaan's clerks are not finished counting before the next season's fleet appears on the horizon.
codex.chr-changchun-audience.body: Qiu Chuji, summoned west by Chinggis Khan, answered that there is a way to guard life, but no medicine of immortality. Li Zhichang wrote the journey down; the frank reply became a touchstone of the steppe road.
codex.chr-changchun-audience.name: Changchun's Audience
codex.chr-daoyi-gulong.body: Wang Dayuan (1349) notes Guli on the western ocean: a meeting-place of foreign ships, a king who honours Buddha, elephant and ox, and brokers who fix a price once and do not change it. Pepper, coconut and western cloth are its staples.
codex.chr-daoyi-gulong.name: Dao Yi Zhi Lue · Calicut
codex.chr-xingcha-malacca.body: Fei Xin, sailing with Zheng He, records that Malacca was raised from a Siamese dependency to a kingdom by Yongle patent. Treasure ships raised stockades and warehouses here. The people follow Islam; the harbour faces the open sea.
codex.chr-xingcha-malacca.name: Xingcha Shenglan · Malacca
codex.chr-yelu-xiyou.body: Yelü Chucai followed the Khan into the lands beyond the Altai and wrote a short geography of cities and products, fearing later ages would forget what the campaign had seen. His prose is spare; it pairs with Changchun's longer road.
codex.chr-yelu-xiyou.name: Yelü Chucai · Record of a Journey West
codex.chr-zhenla-city.body: Zhou Daguan, following a Yuan embassy to Zhenla, describes a square city of stone towers and five gates, each watched by stone Buddhas. Trade, he says, is often done by women; a Tang man who settles there may take a local wife who knows the market.
codex.chr-zhenla-city.name: Zhenla Fengtu Ji · The Walled City
codex.cx-aden.body: You must know that in the province of ADEN there is a Prince who is called the Soldan. The people are all Saracens and adorers of Mahommet, and have a great hatred of Christians. There are many towns and villages in the country.
codex.cx-aden.name: Aden
codex.cx-astrodice.body: You learned the star-dice in two harbours: the pilot of Ormus keeps planet, sign, and house dice in a leather cup, and the reader at Tauris sets the same three beside the card table. The cast is for the hour of departure — the timing of a voyage, not luck, though sailors still call a bright throw great fortune. The houses speak of the road as it will be when you take it.
codex.cx-astrodice.name: The Star-Dice of Tauris
codex.cx-badashan.body: Badashan is a Province inhabited by people who worship Mahommet, and have a peculiar language. It forms a very great kingdom, and the royalty is hereditary. All those of the royal blood are descended from King Alexander and the daughter of King Darius, who was Lord of the vast Empire of Persia.
codex.cx-badashan.name: Badashan
codex.cx-balc.body: Balc is a noble city and a great, though it was much greater in former days. But the Tartars and other nations have greatly ravaged and destroyed it. There were formerly many fine palaces and buildings of marble, and the ruins of them still remain.
codex.cx-balc.name: Balc
codex.cx-baldacum.body: Baudas is a great city, which used to be the seat of the Calif of all the Saracens in the world, just as Rome is the seat of the Pope of all the Christians. A very great river flows through the city, and by this you can descend to the Sea of India.
codex.cx-baldacum.name: Baudas
codex.cx-cacanfu.body: Cacanfu is a noble city. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead; they have paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts. For they have plenty of silk from which they weave stuffs of silk and gold, and sendals in large quantities.
codex.cx-cacanfu.name: Cacanfu
codex.cx-cachanfu.body: When you leave the castle, and travel about 20 miles westward, you come to a river called CARAMORAN, so big that no bridge can be thrown across it; for it is of immense width and depth, and reaches to the Great Ocean that encircles the Universe,—I mean the whole earth.
codex.cx-cachanfu.name: Cachanfu
codex.cx-caiju.body: Caiju is a small city towards the south-east. The people are subject to the Great Kaan and have paper-money. It stands upon the river before mentioned. At this place are collected great quantities of corn and rice to be transported to the great city of Cambaluc for the use of the Kaan’s Court;
codex.cx-caiju.name: Caiju
codex.cx-cail.body: Cail is a great and noble city, and belongs to ASHAR, the eldest of the five brother Kings. It is at this city that all the ships touch that come from the west, as from Hormos and from Kis and from Aden, and all Arabia, laden with horses and with other things for sale.
codex.cx-cail.name: Cail
codex.cx-calatu.body: Calatu is a great city, within a gulf which bears the name of the Gulf of Calatu. It is a noble city, and lies 600 miles from Dufar towards the north-west, upon the sea-shore. The people are Saracens, and are subject to Hormos.
codex.cx-calatu.name: Calatu
codex.cx-camadi.body: After you have ridden down hill those two days, you find yourself in a vast plain, and at the beginning thereof there is a city called CAMADI, which formerly was a great and noble place, but now is of little consequence, for the Tartars in their incursions have several times ravaged it.
codex.cx-camadi.name: Camadi
codex.cx-cambaet.body: Cambaet is a great kingdom lying further west. The people are Idolaters, and have a language of their own, and a king of their own, and are tributary to nobody. The North Star is here still more clearly visible; and henceforward the further you go west the higher you see it.
codex.cx-cambaet.name: Cambaet
codex.cx-cambaluc.body: You must know that the city of Cambaluc hath such a multitude of houses, and such a vast population inside the walls and outside, that it seems quite past all possibility. There is a suburb outside each of the gates, which are twelve in number;
codex.cx-cambaluc.name: Cambaluc
codex.cx-campichu.body: Campichu is also a city of Tangut, and a very great and noble one. Indeed it is the capital and place of government of the whole province of Tangut.
codex.cx-campichu.name: Campichu
codex.cx-camul.body: Camul is a province which in former days was a kingdom. It contains numerous towns and villages, but the chief city bears the name of CAMUL. The province lies between the two deserts;
codex.cx-camul.name: Camul
codex.cx-caracoron.body: Caracoron is a city of some three miles in compass. [It is surrounded by a strong earthen rampart, for stone is scarce there.
codex.cx-caracoron.name: Caracoron
codex.cx-cascar.body: Cascar is a region lying between north-east and east, and constituted a kingdom in former days, but now it is subject to the Great Kaan. The people worship Mahommet. There are a good number of towns and villages, but the greatest and finest is Cascar itself.
codex.cx-cascar.name: Cascar
codex.cx-chamba.body: You must know that on leaving the port of Zayton you sail west-south-west for 1500 miles, and then you come to a country called CHAMBA, a very rich region, having a king of its own.
codex.cx-chamba.name: Chamba
codex.cx-chandu.body: And when you have ridden three days from the city last mentioned, between north-east and north, you come to a city called CHANDU, which was built by the Kaan now reigning.
codex.cx-chandu.name: Chandu
codex.cx-charchan.body: Charchan is a Province of Great Turkey, lying between north-east and east. The people worship Mahommet. There are numerous towns and villages, and the chief city of the kingdom bears its name, Charchan.
codex.cx-charchan.name: Charchan
codex.cx-chinangli.body: Chinangli is a city of Cathay as you go south, and it belongs to the Great Kaan; the people are Idolaters, and have paper-money. There runs through the city a great and wide river, on which a large traffic in silk goods and spices and other costly merchandize passes up and down.
codex.cx-chinangli.name: Chinangli
codex.cx-chinghianfu.body: Chinghianfu is a city of Manzi. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by handicrafts and trade. They have plenty of silk, from which they make sundry kinds of stuffs of silk and gold. There are great and wealthy merchants in the place;
codex.cx-chinghianfu.name: Chinghianfu
codex.cx-chinginju.body: Leaving the city of Chinghianfu and travelling three days south-east through a constant succession of busy and thriving towns and villages, you arrive at the great and noble city of CHINGINJU. The people are Idolaters, use paper-money, and are subject to the Great Kaan.
codex.cx-chinginju.name: Chinginju
codex.cx-cobinan.body: Cobinan is a large town. The people worship Mahommet. There is much Iron and Steel and _Ondanique_, and they make steel mirrors of great size and beauty. They also prepare both _Tutia_ (a thing very good for the eyes) and _Spodium_; and I will tell you the process.
codex.cx-cobinan.name: Cobinan
codex.cx-coiganju.body: Coiganju is, as I have told you already, a very large city standing at the entrance to Manzi. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They have a vast amount of shipping, as I mentioned before in speaking of the River Caramoran.
codex.cx-coiganju.name: Coiganju
codex.cx-coilum.body: When you quit Maabar and go 500 miles towards the south-west you come to the kingdom of COILUM. The people are Idolaters, but there are also some Christians and some Jews. The natives have a language of their own, and a King of their own, and are tributary to no one.
codex.cx-coilum.name: Coilum
codex.cx-cotan.body: Cotan is a province lying between north-east and east, and is eight days’ journey in length. The people are subject to the Great Kaan, and are all worshippers of Mahommet.
codex.cx-cotan.name: Cotan
codex.cx-desert-of-lop.body: Men say of the Desert of Lop that no one could ride across it in a year, and where it is narrowest it still takes a month; it is all sand and barren mountains, with nothing at all to eat. Travellers who mean to cross rest a week at Lop and load provision for a month for man and beast, since in a day and a night you find sweet water enough for fifty or a hundred persons with their beasts. The walls of the caravanserai keep the record of the crossing: names of travellers who made it, prayers for those who did not, and the monks' charcoal account of the days between wells and the bad water.
codex.cx-desert-of-lop.name: Desert Of Lop
codex.cx-desert-voices.body: If you cross the Desert of Lop by night and chance to lag behind your company or fall asleep, when you try to rejoin it you hear spirits talking in the air, and the voices seem to be those of your companions. Sometimes they call you by name; a traveller may be led away so that he never finds his party again, and many have perished in this way. Even by daylight you may hear these spirit-voices, and now and then the sound of instruments — drums, fifes — playing in the air. Such are the perils of the Desert of Lop.
codex.cx-desert-voices.name: Desert Voices
codex.cx-dufar.body: Dufar is a great and noble and fine city, and lies 500 miles to the north-west of Esher. The people are Saracens, and have a Count for their chief, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden; for this city still belongs to the Province of Aden.
codex.cx-dufar.name: Dufar
codex.cx-egrigaia.body: Starting again from Erguiul you ride eastward for eight days, and then come to a province called EGRIGAIA, containing numerous cities and villages, and belonging to Tangut. The capital city is called CALACHAN.
codex.cx-egrigaia.name: Egrigaia
codex.cx-esher.body: Esher is a great city lying in a north-westerly direction from the last, and 400 miles distant from the Port of Aden. It has a king, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden. He has a number of towns and villages under him, and administers his territory well and justly. The people are Saracens.
codex.cx-esher.name: Esher
codex.cx-etzina.body: When you leave the city of Campichu you ride for twelve days, and then reach a city called ETZINA, which is towards the north on the verge of the Sandy Desert; it belongs to the Province of Tangut.
codex.cx-etzina.name: Etzina
codex.cx-fadlan-aurora.body: On your first night in these northern latitudes the horizon turned a brilliant red before the sun had fully set. Above you, a bank of mist held the shapes of horsemen with lances, and a second cloud advanced as if to charge the first. Your companions prayed; the Turkic herders only laughed and said the sky armies fight every evening. You stood watch and recorded what you saw, and the account was written down before the hour turned.
codex.cx-fadlan-aurora.name: The Sky Armies
codex.cx-fadlan-barter.body: At a forest clearing you watched merchants lay bare blades and cow bones upon the snow, mark each pile, and withdraw out of sight. When they returned, sable skins lay beside some goods while others stood untouched. Footprints in the drifts showed long boards tied to the feet of men who never showed their faces. You recorded the rules of the silent exchange.
codex.cx-fadlan-barter.name: Silent Barter
codex.cx-fadlan-bulghar.body: You reached a seasonal market where Bulghar brokers traded honey, wax, arrows, birch wood, and furs of every grade. Grey squirrel and ermine hung beside fish teeth and amber brought from rivers you have not yet seen. You walked the rows and catalogued what the north exports; the list ran longer than your ink would comfortably hold.
codex.cx-fadlan-bulghar.name: The Bulghar Market
codex.cx-fadlan-burial.body: From a bluff above the river you watched without approaching: a great man lay in a boat-shaped grave, dressed for the road ahead, with horses sacrificed and their heads set on stakes. An old woman called the Angel of Death moved among the company, arranging what must be done before the pyre was lit. You recorded the stages of the rite in order, and did not speak ill of what you could not fully understand.
codex.cx-fadlan-burial.name: The Fire-Burial of the Rus
codex.cx-fadlan-captives.body: You met a coffle of captives driven north under guard — men and women bound wrist to wrist, some barefoot on the frozen track. The guard said they were bound for the Bulghar market and beyond. You could not undo the chain; you walked beside them a mile, recorded names and numbers as you could, and wrote what you saw. The account is set down before the hour turns.
codex.cx-fadlan-captives.name: A Coffle on the Forest Road
codex.cx-fadlan-caspian.body: Traders at a caravan halt spoke of Abū Hāmid's voyage among the Caspian isles — a mountain of black clay, an island where sea birds nest among serpents unharmed, and another where only voices are heard. One man claimed his uncle saw the Island of Sheep, where mountain ewes stand thick as locusts. You paid a sailor for a rough chart of the island routes and weighed whether to alter your course toward the coast.
codex.cx-fadlan-caspian.name: The Islands of the Caspian
codex.cx-fadlan-cold.body: You have come to know the north by its cold. The Jayhun lay frozen seventeen spans thick, and horses, mules, and laden carts moved upon it as upon a paved road while your breath hung white before your face. Mid-winter you wore three coats and could not mount without help; water froze in your beard, and every drink began as ice melted in a cauldron. The Itil stood solid enough to cut blocks from. A Turkic woman taught you two pairs of felt boots over horse-hide soles, for cold enters through the feet before the chest. At night the ice boomed beneath you — the guide said the river speaks when the night air falls faster than the water below.
codex.cx-fadlan-cold.name: The Cold of the North
codex.cx-fadlan-darkness.body: Fur merchants who have entered the Land of Darkness told you how they rope themselves wrist to wrist before stepping into the mist where sun and moon never show. A man who loses the line is not found again. They lay out blades and goods, then retreat; when they return, pelts lie beside what they left. You learned how the line is tied and how the goods are marked, and you weigh whether any profit is worth that mist.
codex.cx-fadlan-darkness.name: The Land of Darkness
codex.cx-fadlan-enclosed.body: A Novgorod merchant told how his servant reached the Iughra and heard cries within mountains that slope to the sea. Through a narrow opening, unseen hands pointed at iron blades and left furs in exchange. He believes them the nations Alexander walled away, though no one has seen their faces. You wrote the tale as you heard it, without embellishment.
codex.cx-fadlan-enclosed.name: The Nations of the Enclosed Mountains
codex.cx-fadlan-furs.body: Bulghar brokers spread their wares: beaver and ermine from the northern rivers, and tusks dug from the earth white as snow and heavy as lead. No one agreed what beast left them; some said the bones of ancient peoples, others trade goods bound for Khwarazm. On the sledge road you met a train of black fox and sable pressed in oilcloth, come down the Khazar river from Burtas country, bound for Darband and beyond. You noted the marks of origin; the weight of fur is warmth itself.
codex.cx-fadlan-furs.name: Furs of the Northern Rivers
codex.cx-fadlan-gog.body: Around the evening fire a merchant retold how the Bulghar king once rode to the Itil in flood season and found a man swimming — twelve cubits tall, with a head like the largest cooking pot. Messengers from Wīsū, three months distant, wrote that he belonged to the people of Gog and Magog beyond the sea. You marked the tale as hearsay, yet asked whether any living man had seen such a figure. The north keeps such stories close.
codex.cx-fadlan-gog.name: Tales of Gog and Magog
codex.cx-fadlan-iram.body: A Khwarazmian pilgrim told of a canyon eight farsakhs from the city where a mound rises from stagnant water, topped by a dome bright with gold tiles. Men say it is Iram of the pillars, or a mosque enchanted by the giants of old who marched north from Ad. Anything that touches the water vanishes, and no boat thrown upon it is ever seen again. You turned aside two days toward the canyon marvel.
codex.cx-fadlan-iram.name: Iram of the Pillars
codex.cx-fadlan-khazar.body: Travellers from Itil spoke of two rulers: a king who leads armies, and a khaqan who lives sequestered in the inner palace and never mounts a horse. When famine or defeat comes, the people may demand the khaqan's life, saying his reign has brought ill fortune. You recorded the court customs as Mas'udi described them, and wondered how long the office can endure.
codex.cx-fadlan-khazar.name: The Court of the Khazar Khaqan
codex.cx-fadlan-khwarazm.body: You turned south-west with a party bound for Khwarazm, where Abū Hāmid once sailed the Caspian and came home by a hundred farsakhs of orchards. The brokers promised melons sweet as honey kept through winter, and grapes as large as dates. The steppe lay behind you; ahead the towns grew denser and the wind milder. You entered Khwarazm and rested in the melon markets.
codex.cx-fadlan-khwarazm.name: The Orchards of Khwarazm
codex.cx-fadlan-koumiss.body: A Turkic host offered you a bowl of koumiss fermented one day and one night — still mild, still lawful to drink without intoxication. He waited until you had tasted before he spoke of the road ahead. You accepted the bowl, drank once, and asked his blessing on the road, for to refuse the bowl is to refuse the tent.
codex.cx-fadlan-koumiss.name: The Host's Bowl
codex.cx-fadlan-kurgan.body: Beside the track rose a kurgan already breached — prior diggers had left bones and broken pottery scattered down the slope. The elders said the mound had held a horse lord of an earlier age. You surveyed the mound and sketched what the diggers left; nothing of value remained, only the wind in the hollow crown.
codex.cx-fadlan-kurgan.name: An Opened Tumulus
codex.cx-fadlan-midnight-sun.body: In Bulghar country the twilight lingered so long that a man could scarcely boil a pot between sunset and dawn. A timekeeper swore the shortest night was four and a half hours, and farther north still less. You stayed awake one full cycle and measured the light; sleep comes oddly when the sky never fully darkens.
codex.cx-fadlan-midnight-sun.name: The Night That Barely Comes
codex.cx-fadlan-omen.body: Mid-march, the sun thinned to a crescent and the steppe darkened though it was not yet evening. Some riders shouted that heaven warned the caravan; others said the astronomers of Bukhara had predicted it. The horses shied and would not line until the light returned. You recorded the hour and what the riders said, and saw how the sky itself becomes an omen on open grass.
codex.cx-fadlan-omen.name: The Steppe Eclipse
codex.cx-fadlan-radhaniya.body: At a steppe crossing you met Radhaniya merchants who spoke Arabic, Persian, and Frankish in one breath, and Rus traders with beaver pelts and bare sword blanks. The one party came by camel from Faramā; the other by river from the farthest Slavic forests. Their routes meet here as Ibn Khurradādhbih once mapped them. You shared road news and paid for a written list of safe halts on the Rus road.
codex.cx-fadlan-radhaniya.name: The Radhaniya Road
codex.cx-fadlan-salt.body: A slow train of camels passed, each bearing slabs of salt crust from the shallow southern sea; the drivers said the water recedes in summer and leaves white fields hard enough to cut with an axe. They trade the salt north for fish and south for millet. Later you saw water shining on the horizon — reeds, birds, the ripple of wind — yet the nearer you rode, the more the ground crunched white underhoof. It was a salt flat, not a lake, and the caravan turned aside lest the hooves break through the shell into brine.
codex.cx-fadlan-salt.name: Salt and the Aral Shores
codex.cx-fadlan-sibir.body: An official from Bulghar spoke of Sibir and Julmān beyond Afīkūn, where snow covers house and plain six months of the year. Some say Alexander raised a tower at the edge of the world; others only that the cold wastes men until they boil the same bones seven times. You asked the marching days between Bulghar and Sibir; the names felt very far.
codex.cx-fadlan-sibir.name: Sibir and the Tower
codex.cx-fadlan-sleds.body: Biruni's account came alive before you: men drag provisions on wooden sleighs, or let great dogs pull them, and others glide on bone skates across crusted snow. A relay master offered to carry your pack one day's journey to the next post. You paid for the dog sled relay and marked what the dogs know about the ice that no rider does.
codex.cx-fadlan-sleds.name: Dog Sleds and Bone Skates
codex.cx-fadlan-wall.body: An old courier retold how Sallām the Interpreter left Samarra with felt coats and fur boots to find the barrier raised by Dhū al-Qarnayn. Letter followed letter — Armenia, the Alan king, the Khazar tarkhān — until the earth turned black and smelled of rank soil. You asked which passes still lead toward the northern barrier, and wondered whether any wall still stands between the settled lands and the peoples of the far north.
codex.cx-fadlan-wall.name: The Wall of the Barrier
codex.cx-fanfang.body: A street of the port given over to the merchants of India, Persia and the Arab lands, with their own houses of prayer standing within hearing of the sea-goddess's gongs.
codex.cx-fanfang.name: The Foreign Quarter
codex.cx-four-pillars.body: You learned the four pillars from a calendar master at Baldacum. He reads a time in four columns, and from them a three-year travel window: a way that lies shut this season may lie open in the next. The master reads the years the road is open, so a journey may be timed to a window that will carry it. The pillars speak in years, and the choice stays yours.
codex.cx-four-pillars.name: Four Pillars
codex.cx-fuju.body: Now this city of Fuju is the key of the kingdom which is called CHONKA, and which is one of the nine great divisions of Manzi. The city is a seat of great trade and great manufactures. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan.
codex.cx-fuju.name: Fuju
codex.cx-geomancy.body: You learned the sixteen figures from the sand-reader of Baldacum, who marks them in the dust — which open a road, which stop it, and which hold you a day. At Alexandria the same art casts near the warehouses for risk on the sea lanes and the desert posts alike, and you learned to ask what Populus means for a voyage. He spoke great fortune and great ill omen without shame; the sand does.
codex.cx-geomancy.name: The Sixteen Figures
codex.cx-hexagrams.body: You learned the hexagrams from a chronologer of the Astronomical Bureau at Cambaluc, who sat with you fourteen days and taught the casting of hexagrams for the road. He does not ask after fortune. He asks after time and position — which season a road is open, and where a man stands when he chooses it. The cast sets the standing of the moment, and the reading is that.
codex.cx-hexagrams.name: Hexagrams
codex.cx-hundred-shiploads.body: For every shipload of pepper that reaches Alexandria bound for Christendom, a hundred come in to Zayton. It is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.
codex.cx-hundred-shiploads.name: A Hundred Shiploads
codex.cx-jade-rivers.body: The jade of Lop's market comes down from the streams above Cotan, where the waters run from the snow mountains and lay their gravel bare when the autumn rivers fall. The best stones are gathered in the weeks when the water is low, and the dealers keep them on black velvet to show the colour — a piece of mutton-fat white jade the size of a man's fist costs more than a camel. A man who knows the season may buy at the source for a tenth of the bazaar price; the rivers run east, and their course bends toward Sachiu.
codex.cx-jade-rivers.name: Jade Rivers
codex.cx-jiaobei.body: You learned the temple cups from the reader at Kinsay, and found them waiting at Zayton's temple threshold. The cups give three answers — leave, refuse, or ask again. A bright answer is called great fortune; a dark one, great ill omen — and still you must choose a road. When the cups laugh, she said, that is not failure; it is the craft admitting it has no counsel yet.
codex.cx-jiaobei.name: The Cups of Zayton
codex.cx-kenjanfu.body: And when you leave the city of Cachanfu of which I have spoken, and travel eight days westward, you meet with cities and boroughs abounding in trade and industry, and quantities of beautiful trees, and gardens, and fine plains planted with mulberries, which are the trees on the leaves of which the s
codex.cx-kenjanfu.name: Kenjanfu
codex.cx-kerman.body: Kerman is a kingdom which is also properly in Persia, and formerly it had a hereditary prince. Since the Tartars conquered the country the rule is no longer hereditary, but the Tartar sends to administer whatever lord he pleases.
codex.cx-kerman.name: Kerman
codex.cx-keshimur.body: Keshimur also is a Province inhabited by a people who are Idolaters and have a language of their own. They have an astonishing acquaintance with the devilries of enchantment; insomuch that they make their idols to speak.
codex.cx-keshimur.name: Keshimur
codex.cx-kinsay.body: When you have left the city of Changan and have travelled for three days through a splendid country, passing a number of towns and villages, you arrive at the most noble city of KINSAY, a name which is as much as to say in our tongue “The City of Heaven,” as I told you before.
codex.cx-kinsay.name: Kinsay
codex.cx-linju.body: On leaving the city of Sinju-matu you travel for eight days towards the south, always coming to great and rich towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. The people are all subjects of the Great Kaan, use paper-money, and burn their dead.
codex.cx-linju.name: Linju
codex.cx-lots.body: The cylinder is shaken until a single numbered slip falls out. The number is read against a book of verses. The verse does not answer the question asked; it names the thing the asker had not weighed.
codex.cx-lots.name: Reading the Slips
codex.cx-maabar.body: When you leave the Island of Seilan and sail westward about 60 miles, you come to the great province of MAABAR which is styled INDIA THE GREATER; it is best of all the Indies and is on the mainland. You must know that in this province there are five kings, who are own brothers.
codex.cx-maabar.name: Maabar
codex.cx-melibar.body: Melibar is a great kingdom lying towards the west. The people are Idolaters; they have a language of their own, and a king of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. In this country you see more of the North Star, for it shows two cubits above the water.
codex.cx-melibar.name: Melibar
codex.cx-mien.body: And when you have travelled those 15 days through such a difficult country as I have described, in which travellers have to carry provisions for the road because there are no inhabitants, then you arrive at the capital city of this Province of Mien, and it also is called AMIEN, and is a very great a
codex.cx-mien.name: Mien
codex.cx-monsoon.body: The wind of the Indian sea turns with the seasons. Ships out of Zayton for the Indies wait upon it, and a master who sails against it does not come back to say so.
codex.cx-monsoon.name: The Monsoon
codex.cx-nanghin.body: Nanghin is a very noble Province towards the west. The people are Idolaters (and so forth) and live by trade and manufactures. They have silk in great abundance, and they weave many fine tissues of silk and gold.
codex.cx-nanghin.name: Nanghin
codex.cx-ormus.body: The Plain of which we have spoken extends in a southerly direction for five days’ journey, and then you come to another descent some twenty miles in length, where the road is very bad and full of peril, for there are many robbers and bad characters about.
codex.cx-ormus.name: Ormus
codex.cx-paukin.body: When you leave Coiganju you ride south-east for a day along a causeway laid with fine stone, which you find at this entrance to Manzi. On either hand there is a great expanse of water, so that you cannot enter the province except along this causeway.
codex.cx-paukin.name: Paukin
codex.cx-pein.body: Pein is a province five days in length, lying between east and north-east. The people are worshippers of Mahommet, and subjects of the Great Kaan. There are a good number of towns and villages, but the most noble is PEIN, the capital of the kingdom.
codex.cx-pein.name: Pein
codex.cx-pentam.body: When you leave Locac and sail for 500 miles towards the south, you come to an island called PENTAM, a very wild place. All the wood that grows thereon consists of odoriferous trees. There is no more to say about it; so let us sail about sixty miles further between those two Islands.
codex.cx-pentam.name: Pentam
codex.cx-pepper-freight.body: Thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on lignaloes and sandalwood and other bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper.
codex.cx-pepper-freight.name: Freight Rates at Zayton
codex.cx-road-23.body: You read how Barca came on with three hundred and fifty thousand horse and encamped on the plain within ten miles of Alau. He addressed his men, declaring his intention of fighting after three days, and his confidence of success: for they were in the right, and had fifty thousand men more than the enemy.
codex.cx-road-23.name: How Barca and His Army Advanced to Meet Alau
codex.cx-road-24.body: You record the usual description of their advance to meet one another, with no circumstance singled out. Toctai is joined by the two sons of Totamangu with a goodly company, and the two hosts encamp within ten miles of each other on the Plain of Nerghi.
codex.cx-road-24.name: How Toctai Marched Against Nogai
codex.cx-road-25.body: You note how the second embassy ends in open defiance: the messengers carry a threat of attack should Nogai refuse to present himself before Toctai, and Nogai refuses with defiance. Both sides prepare for war, and Toctai's force is the greater in numbers.
codex.cx-road-25.name: Second Message That Toctai Sent to Nogai
codex.cx-road-26.body: The chronicle gives the whole of this in the usual formula, with no circumstance worth transcribing; you set it down for the record all the same. Two things stand out: Nogai's forces, though inferior in numbers, are the better men-at-arms; and King Toctai shows great valour.
codex.cx-road-26.name: How Toctai and Nogai Address Their People
codex.cx-road-27.body: Alau calls together a numerous parliament of his worthies and addresses them. The chronicle keeps the old French phrase — he assembled again a parliament of a great quantity of good men — and you copy it into your record as the surest form of the fact.
codex.cx-road-27.name: How Alau Addressed His Followers
codex.cx-road-28.body: You find the great battle between Alau and Barca described in the usual style, with nothing characteristic to single out; only the end stands clear — the rout of Barca, and great slaughter. No circumstance of the field is set down, and none is yours to invent.
codex.cx-road-28.name: Great Battle Between Alau and Barca
codex.cx-road-29.body: The Christians, hearing what the Calif had said, were in great dismay, but they lifted all their hopes to God their Creator, that He would help them in their strait. Their wisest took counsel together — among them a number of bishops and priests — and found no resource but to turn to Him from whom all good things come, beseeching Him to protect them from the cruel hands of the Calif.
codex.cx-road-29.name: Christians Were in Great Dismay Because of What the Calif Had Said
codex.cx-road-30.body: When the vision had visited the bishop several times, he related the whole matter to the Christians, and with one consent they called the cobbler before them. They told him it was their wish that he should pray, for God had promised to accomplish the matter by his means. He made many excuses, declaring he was not so good a man as they represented; but they persisted with so much sweetness that at last he said he would not tarry, but do what they desired.
codex.cx-road-30.name: One-Eyed Cobler Was Desired to Pray for the Christians
codex.cx-runes.body: You learned twenty-four birch staves from the carver at Kiovia, who cuts a mark into birch before every ford and reads the winter roads. When Fehu falls he names great fortune; when Hagalaz does, great ill omen. At Caffa a northern trader casts the same marks on the quay for the steppe road inland, and you learned how a single rune is drawn, and what Raidho names on the quay.
codex.cx-runes.name: Runic Staves of the North
codex.cx-saianfu.body: Saianfu is a very great and noble city, and it rules over twelve other large and rich cities, and is itself a seat of great trade and manufacture. The people are Idolaters (and so forth). They have much silk, from which they weave fine silken stuffs;
codex.cx-saianfu.name: Saianfu
codex.cx-samarcanda.body: Samarcan is a great and noble city towards the north-west, inhabited by both Christians and Saracens, who are subject to the Great Kaan’s nephew, CAIDOU by name; he is, however, at bitter enmity with the Kaan. I will tell you of a great marvel that happened at this city.
codex.cx-samarcanda.name: Samarcanda
codex.cx-sapurgan.body: On leaving the Castle, you ride over fine plains and beautiful valleys, and pretty hill-sides producing excellent grass pasture, and abundance of fruits, and all other products. Armies are glad to take up their quarters here on account of the plenty that exists.
codex.cx-sapurgan.name: Sapurgan
codex.cx-sea-goddess.body: A goddess of this coast to whom shipmasters go before sailing. Her temple keeps a cylinder of numbered slips; a slip is drawn and read against a book of verses.
codex.cx-sea-goddess.name: The Goddess of the Sea
codex.cx-semenat.body: Semenat is a great kingdom towards the west. The people are Idolaters, and have a king and a language of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. They are not corsairs, but live by trade and industry as honest people ought. It is a place of very great trade.
codex.cx-semenat.name: Semenat
codex.cx-siju.body: When you leave Piju you travel towards the south for two days, through beautiful districts abounding in everything, and in which you find quantities of all kinds of game. At the end of those two days you reach the city of SIJU, a great, rich, and noble city, flourishing with trade and manufactures.
codex.cx-siju.name: Siju
codex.cx-sindafu.body: When you have travelled those 20 days westward through the mountains, as I have told you, then you arrive at a plain belonging to a province called Sindafu, which still is on the confines of Manzi, and the capital city of which is (also) called SINDAFU.
codex.cx-sindafu.name: Sindafu
codex.cx-sinju.body: You must know that when you leave the city of Yanju, after going 15 miles south-east, you come to a city called SINJU, of no great size, but possessing a very great amount of shipping and trade. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and use paper-money.
codex.cx-sinju.name: Sinju
codex.cx-sinjumatu.body: On leaving Tadinfu you travel three days towards the south, always finding numbers of noble and populous towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. There is also abundance of game in the country, and everything in profusion.
codex.cx-sinjumatu.name: Sinjumatu
codex.cx-steppe-road.body: Before the Gate of the Turks, caravan masters spoke of an akilavuz — a guide bred to these roads, who knows where the snow lies knee-deep and which ribāt still keeps fodder; without him you may wander ten days on the steppe and meet no soul. The road itself is crossings: hide boats stretched on saddle frames where rivers run too swift for wading, a crossroads where Radhaniya and Rus routes meet, and low yurts where a sick child waits for water and herbs while the caravan master signals to move. You have written all of it down as part of the road.
codex.cx-steppe-road.name: The Steppe Road
codex.cx-suju.body: Suju is a very great and noble city. The people are Idolaters, subjects of the Great Kaan, and have paper-money. They possess silk in great quantities, from which they make gold brocade and other stuffs, and they live by their manufactures and trade.
codex.cx-suju.name: Suju
codex.cx-taican.body: After those twelve days’ journey you come to a fortified place called TAICAN, where there is a great corn market. It is a fine place, and the mountains that you see towards the south are all composed of salt.
codex.cx-taican.name: Taican
codex.cx-tana.body: Tana is a great kingdom lying towards the west, a kingdom great both in size and worth. The people are Idolaters, with a language of their own, and a king of their own, and tributary to nobody. No pepper grows there, nor other spices, but plenty of incense; not the white kind however, but brown.
codex.cx-tana.name: Tana
codex.cx-tangut-rites.body: After thirty days of desert you come to Sachiu, in the province of Tangut, a city lying on the edge of the Great Desert where the caravans restock after the terrible crossing. The people are for the most part Idolaters, with a peculiar language of their own; they are no traders, but live by the fruits of the earth. They have many abbeys and minsters, all full of idols of divers fashions, to which they pay great honour and show reverence. Their dead are burned on pyres, and the ashes are gathered and kept — you watched a burial and set it down in your book.
codex.cx-tangut-rites.name: Tangut Rites
codex.cx-tanpiju.body: When you leave Kinsay and travel a day’s journey to the south-east, through a plenteous region, passing a succession of dwellings and charming gardens, you reach the city of TANPIJU, a great, rich, and fine city, under Kinsay.
codex.cx-tanpiju.name: Tanpiju
codex.cx-tarot.body: You learned the tarot from a Frankish widow at Tauris. Her spreads weigh gain against cost, and the rule of choice at forks — when two post-roads split, you lay a choice-gate and compare what each road would gain and what it would cost. She does not name the outcome. She weighs the choice before it is made.
codex.cx-tarot.name: Tarot
codex.cx-tauris.body: Tauris is a great and noble city, situated in a great province called YRAC, in which are many other towns and villages. But as Tauris is the most noble I will tell you about it.
codex.cx-tauris.name: Tauris
codex.cx-tenduc.body: Tenduc is a province which lies towards the east, and contains numerous towns and villages; among which is the chief city, also called TENDUC. The king of the province is of the lineage of Prester John, George by name, and he holds the land under the Great Kaan;
codex.cx-tenduc.name: Tenduc
codex.cx-tiju.body: When you leave Cayu, you ride another day to the south-east through a constant succession of villages and fields and fine farms until you come to TIJU, which is a city of no great size but abounding in everything. The people are Idolaters (and so forth).
codex.cx-tiju.name: Tiju
codex.cx-yarcan.body: Yarcan is a province five days’ journey in extent. The people follow the Law of Mahommet, but there are also Nestorian and Jacobite Christians. They are subject to the same Prince that I mentioned, the Great Kaan’s nephew. They have plenty of everything, [particularly of cotton.
codex.cx-yarcan.name: Yarcan
codex.cx-yasdi.body: Yasdi also is properly in Persia; it is a good and noble city, and has a great amount of trade. They weave there quantities of a certain silk tissue known as _Yasdi_, which merchants carry into many quarters to dispose of. The people are worshippers of Mahommet.
codex.cx-yasdi.name: Yasdi
codex.cx-zayton-tithe.body: Ten in the hundred on all merchandise landed at Zayton, including precious stones and pearls — the Great Kaan takes the tamghā on everything. With the ship's freight added, a merchant pays out half his cargo's worth before he has sold a grain of it.
codex.cx-zayton-tithe.name: The Kaan's Tamghā
codex.cx-zayton-watch.body: The night watch of Zayton keeps its own account of every shadow that slips past the Kaan's clerks. After dark the watch lanterns stop at your lodging and look for your mark in the quay ledger; when they cannot find it, their leader draws no weapon but sets a late-declaration tally on the table. Pay then, or leave the cargo in bond for inspection. The watch writes a name down twice before it is done, and their rounds over the quay are known to you by heart before your cargo is released.
codex.cx-zayton-watch.name: The Night Watch of Zayton
codex.leg-earthly-paradise.body: Some travellers' books place Paradise beyond the deserts of India, guarded so that no living man may enter. The story is older than any one author. Here it stands among legends, not among charts.
codex.leg-earthly-paradise.name: The Earthly Paradise
codex.leg-prester-john.body: Beyond India, say the wonder-books, reigns a Christian prince called Prester John, whose rivers run with gems and whose salamanders live in fire. Mandeville gathers the tale as itinerary; this codex keeps it as legend — origin marked authored, never as a sourced city gate.
codex.leg-prester-john.name: Prester John
div.astrodice.name: Astrodice
div.astrodice.result.00: Great fortune: the dice name a morning departure before the heat rises.
div.astrodice.result.01: The dice name a three-day wait: the next caravan is better company.
div.astrodice.result.02: The dice name the north gate; the south road is crowded with tax clerks.
div.astrodice.result.03: The dice name a short leg only; do not press beyond the next well.
div.astrodice.result.04: The dice name bargaining at dusk, when the stalls lower their first prices.
div.astrodice.result.05: The dice name a translator before any contract is sealed.
div.astrodice.result.06: The dice name inland forage; the coast wind turns against shipping.
div.astrodice.result.07: The dice name lodging near the mosque courtyard, not the riverbank.
div.astrodice.result.08: The dice name paying the toll in full and asking no favours.
div.astrodice.result.09: The dice name sending a scout ahead to the next caravanserai.
div.astrodice.result.10: The dice name postponing the mountain pass until after the new moon.
div.astrodice.result.11: The dice name buying water-skins here; they will be dearer ahead.
div.astrodice.result.12: The dice name travelling with the spice merchants, not alone.
div.astrodice.result.13: The dice name avoiding night watches on the open steppe.
div.astrodice.result.14: The dice name changing horses at the next post, not this one.
div.astrodice.result.15: Ill omen: the dice name postponing the mountain pass until after the new moon.
div.astrodice.result.16: The dice name resting one day for a lame camel rather than forcing the march.
div.astrodice.result.17: The dice name asking the astrologer of this court which month the road opens.
div.astrodice.result.18: The dice name keeping silver divided among three purses.
div.astrodice.result.19: The dice name taking the longer river road; the short cut floods.
div.astrodice.result.20: The dice name waiting for the Friday market before you sell.
div.astrodice.result.21: The dice name speaking little of your destination in this inn.
div.astrodice.result.22: The dice name hiring a local watch for the warehouse night.
div.astrodice.result.23: The dice name not crossing the ferry until the boatmen sober after noon.
div.astrodice.result.24: The dice name reading the wind for two dawns before you sail.
div.astrodice.result.25: The dice name seeking the Armenian quarter for news of the inland road.
div.astrodice.result.26: The dice name not trusting the first guide who greets you at the gate.
div.astrodice.result.27: The dice name marking the wells on your tablet before you leave.
div.astrodice.result.28: The dice name offering a small gift at the shrine before you bargain.
div.astrodice.result.29: The dice name choosing the road that still has shade at noon.
div.bazi-relationship.name: Pillars Compatibility
div.bazi-relationship.result.00: The two charts share the day master: two strong wills; one must yield at the crossroads.
div.bazi-relationship.result.01: Fire meets wood: the elder warms the younger; a caring bond.
div.bazi-relationship.result.02: Water meets wood: the tree drinks deep; the younger grows.
div.bazi-relationship.result.03: Wood meets earth: the branch breaks the soil; a stubborn pair.
div.bazi-relationship.result.04: Earth meets metal: the ore refines; a steady bond.
div.bazi-relationship.result.05: Metal meets water: the blade cools; a calm alliance.
div.bazi-relationship.result.06: The unions are many: a fortunate match; the road together is smooth.
div.bazi-relationship.result.07: The clashes are many: sparks fly; keep the peace with care.
div.bazi-relationship.result.08: The day master is strong in both: two leaders; take turns at the helm.
div.bazi-relationship.result.09: The day master is weak in one: one leans on the other; the load is shared.
div.bazi-relationship.result.10: The hour pillars agree: the day's end is harmonious.
div.bazi-relationship.result.11: The year pillars agree: the elders bless the bond.
div.bazi-relationship.result.12: A moving star in the chart: a change; the bond evolves.
div.bazi-relationship.result.13: The element of water is rich in both: deep feeling; a flowing life.
div.bazi-relationship.result.14: Fire without wood: a flame that falters; feed it with patience.
div.bazi-relationship.result.15: Metal without fire: a cold blade; warm words are needed.
div.bazi-relationship.result.16: A scholar star for one: learning aids the union.
div.bazi-relationship.result.17: A wealth star for one: provision; the household thrives.
div.bazi-relationship.result.18: An officer star for one: duty; a formal bond.
div.bazi-relationship.result.19: A seal star: protection; the bond is sheltered.
div.bazi-relationship.result.20: The peach blossom star: charm; a lively affection.
div.bazi-relationship.result.21: The lonely star for one: solitude before the meeting; patience.
div.bazi-relationship.result.22: A noble star for both: a fortunate pairing; the road smiles.
div.bazi-relationship.result.23: The conflict star: a battle of wills; choose your battles.
div.bazi-relationship.result.24: The union of the sun branches: a natural fit; the journey is easy.
div.bazi-relationship.result.25: The union of the hour branches: the quiet hours are shared.
div.bazi-relationship.result.26: A void in one chart: a gap; speak what is missing.
div.bazi-relationship.result.27: A tomb in one chart: a closing; let the old year end.
div.bazi-relationship.result.28: A child star: a new venture or a child blesses the bond.
div.bazi-relationship.result.29: The two charts balance: an equal road; walk it together.
div.bazi.apprentice: The astrologer studies your birth date with narrowed eyes, drawing a chart of eight characters in black ink. 'Your wood is strong but your fire is weak,' she says. 'This is not a judgment. It is a compass. The roads that suit a fire person will burn you out. The roads that suit a wood person will let you grow. I will teach you to read your own chart — but first you must accept that you cannot walk every road.'
div.bazi.desc: The Four Pillars of Destiny examine the hour, day, month, and year of your birth against the elemental cycles of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water. The chart reveals what kind of traveller you are — which regions suit your nature, which companions strengthen you, and which years bring opportunity. Cost: 400 coins. Horizon: three years.
div.bazi.name: Four Pillars
div.bazi.result.00: Your day-master is firm. Take the steady official road; do not gamble on shortcuts.
div.bazi.result.01: The yearly water is strong; river crossings have a wider window of safe passage.
div.bazi.result.02: Earth energy is full. Stay on the long overland road; avoid switching boats too often.
div.bazi.result.03: Metal energy is strong. Bargain firmly, but do not offend the gate clerks.
div.bazi.result.04: Wood energy rises. Set out early, and ask often about new routes.
div.bazi.result.05: Fire energy is parched. Rest at midday in summer; do not travel under the noon sun.
div.bazi.result.06: The day-pillar advises: hiring an interpreter matters more than meeting a merchant.
div.bazi.result.07: The year-pillar is stable. Longer contracts are worth signing.
div.bazi.result.08: The month-command is weak. Shorten each leg of the journey.
div.bazi.result.09: The hour-pillar stirs. At the fork, cast the coins again before deciding.
div.bazi.result.10: Water is missing from the chart. Choose roads that follow the river.
div.bazi.result.11: Fire is missing from the chart. Camp near settlements at night.
div.bazi.result.12: Competing elements are many. Travel with few companions and clear rules.
div.bazi.result.13: Expressive stars shine. Good for gathering news of goods and market prices.
div.bazi.result.14: Wealth stars are visible. Linger in the market, but not at the posting station.
div.bazi.result.15: Authority stars weigh heavily. Prepare your documents in full before the checkpoint.
div.bazi.result.16: A seal star protects. Lodge in a city that has a temple or monastery.
div.bazi.result.17: A luck cycle change approaches. Delay any major change of route.
div.bazi.result.18: This chart says: travel east to study, west to trade.
div.bazi.result.19: Your birth season hints: in autumn, depart early; in spring, depart steady.
div.bazi.result.20: The day-branch clashes. Do not share a room or discuss strategy with someone of the same sign.
div.bazi.result.21: Heavenly stems combine. Hire camels together with a partner; do not take it all on your own.
div.bazi.result.22: Earthly branches open. Go slow on mountain paths; speed on the plain.
div.bazi.result.23: Void descends on the road. Do not trust unfounded rumours of a shortcut.
div.bazi.result.24: Salary and blade are both clear. Travel with a familiar merchant group.
div.bazi.result.25: Weather needs water. Take the sea leg before the dry stretch.
div.bazi.result.26: Weather needs fire. Choose valley roads with long hours of sunlight.
div.bazi.result.27: This chart says: for three years, let trade support your learning, not the other way.
div.bazi.result.28: The post-horse star moves. In a year of frequent shifts, lighten your cargo.
div.bazi.result.29: A canopy star descends. Visit a local teacher before settling on a long route.
div.coffee.name: Coffee Grounds
div.coffee.result.00: A bird in the grounds: good news flies toward you.
div.coffee.result.01: A mountain in the grounds: an obstacle; a hard climb, then rest.
div.coffee.result.02: A chain of beads: a necklace of small gains; collect them.
div.coffee.result.03: A hand in the grounds: help from another; take the offered hand.
div.coffee.result.04: An eye in the grounds: a watchful person; be discreet.
div.coffee.result.05: A heart in the grounds: an affection kindles on the road.
div.coffee.result.06: A snake in the grounds: a subtle enemy; keep secrets.
div.coffee.result.07: A tree in the grounds: growth; a venture thrives.
div.coffee.result.08: A sword in the grounds: a sharp decision; cut quickly.
div.coffee.result.09: A ring in the grounds: a bond; a contract or a betrothal.
div.coffee.result.10: A cross in the grounds: a burden; bear it, it will lighten.
div.coffee.result.11: A star in the grounds: guidance; the night sky steers you.
div.coffee.result.12: A boat in the grounds: a crossing; a voyage approaches.
div.coffee.result.13: A horse in the grounds: a fast ride; a journey of urgency.
div.coffee.result.14: A lion in the grounds: courage; face the trial boldly.
div.coffee.result.15: A fish in the grounds: plenty; the market feeds you well.
div.coffee.result.16: A key in the grounds: a solution; a door opens.
div.coffee.result.17: A ladder in the grounds: ascent; a rise in fortune.
div.coffee.result.18: A bell in the grounds: a summons; answer the call.
div.coffee.result.19: A candle in the grounds: a light in darkness; hope holds.
div.coffee.result.20: A crown in the grounds: honor; a position of trust.
div.coffee.result.21: A whip in the grounds: a dispute; keep the peace.
div.coffee.result.22: A mask in the grounds: a disguise; the true intent is hidden.
div.coffee.result.23: A wheel in the grounds: a turning; fortune changes direction.
div.coffee.result.24: A mountain gate in the grounds: a pass; the way narrows, then opens.
div.coffee.result.25: A ship under sail: departure; the time to leave has come.
div.coffee.result.26: A grain stalk: harvest; the long effort pays.
div.coffee.result.27: A wave: emotion; let it pass before you decide.
div.coffee.result.28: A pair of cups: a meeting; two minds agree.
div.coffee.result.29: The grounds clear at the rim: a clean road; go without fear.
div.dream.name: Dream Reading
div.dream.result.00: A gate left open: the road ahead stands ready; set out at first light.
div.dream.result.01: Water rising at the threshold: a crossing is near, but keep your purse laced.
div.dream.result.02: A flock of cranes overhead: good company will join your wagon before noon.
div.dream.result.03: Eating bread alone: the next town offers hospitality if you ask at the well.
div.dream.result.04: A key found in grass: something lost returns, perhaps your direction.
div.dream.result.05: A ship with no sails: delay on this route; the word you wait for has not come.
div.dream.result.06: Climbing a tower: knowledge will raise you — seek the scribe at the shrine.
div.dream.result.07: A door that will not open: the way is barred until you pay the toll or earn the pass.
div.dream.result.08: A burning cart: danger on the western road; sell the goods before you leave.
div.dream.result.09: Teeth falling out: an elder's counsel will be hard to hear but true.
div.dream.result.10: A dead tree blooming: a worn-out venture revives; take it up once more.
div.dream.result.11: Crossing a river in a dream: your wish to travel is sound, but wait one market day.
div.dream.result.12: A wedding feast: an alliance is offered; agree, but name your terms.
div.dream.result.13: A road rising into cloud: the mountain pass is uncertain; hire a guide.
div.dream.result.14: A child laughing: a light heart pays better than gold on the open road.
div.dream.result.15: A purse full of sand: what seems wealth is not; count your silver twice.
div.dream.result.16: A hare racing the wind: hurry, but not so fast you lose your cart.
div.dream.result.17: An empty inn: rest where you find shelter, not where you planned.
div.dream.result.18: A bell without a clapper: your question has no answer yet; ask again at the next city.
div.dream.result.19: A lantern in rain: a small light will see you through the dark marsh.
div.dream.result.20: A horse standing in water: this route will test you; keep the reins short.
div.dream.result.21: A stranger handing you a coin: help comes from an unexpected quarter; take it.
div.dream.result.22: A broken bridge: change course; the ford is three days south.
div.dream.result.23: A field ready for harvest: your cargo will sell well at the next gate.
div.dream.result.24: A shadow following you: trouble stalks your trail; travel with a companion.
div.dream.result.25: A window thrown open: news arrives that changes your route — welcome it.
div.dream.result.26: A snake in the road: do not force this argument; let the dispute settle.
div.dream.result.27: A roof mended with gold: spend on what shelters you; it will be repaid.
div.dream.result.28: A journey in the sky: your ambition is grand; shorten the first leg.
div.dream.result.29: Waking from a dream of departure: the sign favors moving, yet keep your plans to yourself.
div.fengshui.name: Feng Shui
div.fengshui.result.00: The mountain stands behind the house: the road behind is safe; return when needed.
div.fengshui.result.01: A stream before the door: wealth flows toward you; buy at the waterside.
div.fengshui.result.02: The dragon line runs true: a prosperous route; the land itself favors you.
div.fengshui.result.03: A broken dragon line: a hazard ahead; mend your cart before the gorge.
div.fengshui.result.04: A house with a straight road to its door: fortune rushes past; stand aside.
div.fengshui.result.05: A well in the courtyard: a source of refreshment; the inn is honest.
div.fengshui.result.06: A tall tree at the gate: shelter and shade; rest here.
div.fengshui.result.07: A dead tree at the gate: a warning; this place holds no fortune.
div.fengshui.result.08: The water turns at the bend: the fortune turns with it; settle there.
div.fengshui.result.09: A road that curves like a bow: a blessed dwelling; bargain well.
div.fengshui.result.10: A road that pierces like an arrow: ill fortune aims at the door; do not stay.
div.fengshui.result.11: A garden in the south: warmth and growth; plant your plan here.
div.fengshui.result.12: A wall in the north: protection from the cold; winter travel is guarded.
div.fengshui.result.13: An open east: the morning light blesses the departure.
div.fengshui.result.14: A cluttered west: the evening burden; travel light.
div.fengshui.result.15: A pond that stills: patience is repaid; wait a day.
div.fengshui.result.16: A waterfall: loud fortune; a sudden gain, soon spent.
div.fengshui.result.17: A bridge at the gate: a crossing gift; pay the toll gladly.
div.fengshui.result.18: A shrine at the crossroads: the gods of the road watch; offer a coin.
div.fengshui.result.19: A bell tower to the east: the morning bell calls you to rise early.
div.fengshui.result.20: A smithy to the south: sparks and strength; mend your iron here.
div.fengshui.result.21: A mill by the water: the wheel turns; your fortune grinds slowly fine.
div.fengshui.result.22: A graveyard on the hill: the ancestors watch; do no dishonor.
div.fengshui.result.23: A market at the crossing of roads: trade flows; sell before noon.
div.fengshui.result.24: A stable in the east: the horse is ready; a fast start.
div.fengshui.result.25: A garden wall that crumbles: a falling fortune; repair it or leave.
div.fengshui.result.26: A roof that leaks at the corner: a small loss; fix it cheaply now.
div.fengshui.result.27: A door facing the sunset: the day closes early; plan by morning.
div.fengshui.result.28: A window facing the mountain: a clear view; the path is known.
div.fengshui.result.29: The land breathes even: balance; the journey holds neither great risk nor great gain.
div.geomancy.name: Geomancy
div.geomancy.result.00: The figure opens the road if you keep to the caravan hours.
div.geomancy.result.01: Great fortune: the figure opens a side gate; ask the porter for the merchants' entrance.
div.geomancy.result.02: The figure opens trade in salt and hides; leave silks for another city.
div.geomancy.result.03: The figure opens a morning audience; do not wait until the heat.
div.geomancy.result.04: The figure opens the desert road only with two spare water-skins.
div.geomancy.result.05: The figure opens learning the local prayer times before you bargain.
div.geomancy.result.06: The figure opens hiring a watchman for your packs at the inn.
div.geomancy.result.07: The figure opens a short stay; leave before the weekly tax count.
div.geomancy.result.08: The figure opens asking the qadi's clerk which roads are under ban.
div.geomancy.result.09: The figure opens sharing a fire with the next company, not camping alone.
div.geomancy.result.10: The figure holds you one day: mend harness before you go.
div.geomancy.result.11: The figure holds counsel: write the distances between wells tonight.
div.geomancy.result.12: The figure holds: do not sell until you have heard three prices.
div.geomancy.result.13: The figure holds: wait for the dust storm to pass the ridge.
div.geomancy.result.14: The figure holds: keep your letters sealed until the next city.
div.geomancy.result.15: Great ill omen: the figure stops the night march; daylight only on this band.
div.geomancy.result.16: The figure stops a bargain with a man who will not name his city.
div.geomancy.result.17: The figure stops crossing the river at this ford; go upstream.
div.geomancy.result.18: The figure stops trusting maps drawn in another season.
div.geomancy.result.19: The figure stops paying guides who demand half in advance.
div.geomancy.result.20: The figure stops entering the warehouse quarter after dark.
div.geomancy.result.21: The figure stops arguing tolls; pay and keep moving.
div.geomancy.result.22: The figure stops dividing your company on this plain.
div.geomancy.result.23: The figure stops opening wine before the next shrine.
div.geomancy.result.24: The figure stops chasing rumour of a shorter road east.
div.geomancy.result.25: The figure warns: the next well may be guarded; approach with gifts.
div.geomancy.result.26: The figure warns: leave heavy cargo and send a light scout first.
div.geomancy.result.27: The figure warns: do not sleep in the ruined caravanserai.
div.geomancy.result.28: The figure warns: change your planned day of departure by one.
div.geomancy.result.29: The figure warns: ask again after you have seen the sky clear.
div.iching.apprentice: The old scholar unrolls a strip of yellow silk covered with broken and unbroken lines. 'These are not fortunes,' he says. 'They are maps. Each hexagram is a landscape — mountains, rivers, thunder, wind. You do not ask if you will succeed. You ask: which road through this landscape is mine?' He places three coins in your open palm. 'Cast them. We will read what the earth writes.'
div.iching.desc: The Book of Changes reveals the shape of the road ahead. Ask not whether fortune favours you, but which direction aligns with the moment. Cast three coins six times to form a hexagram; each line speaks of movement or stillness. The reading shows which routes open and which close. Cost: 200 coins. Horizon: one season.
div.iching.hex.0.advice: Force favours action with clear purpose. Choose the main road and set out at dawn; do not wait for a companion who hesitates.
div.iching.hex.1.advice: The Field receives what comes. Follow a route that others have travelled and marked; carry less than you think you need.
div.iching.hex.10.advice: The third of three passes opens. The high road is open, the low road is open, the grass is firm. Move without delay.
div.iching.hex.11.advice: Heaven presses earth and doors close. Do not set out against the season; wait three days and try the next station.
div.iching.hex.12.advice: You will find company on this road, even where you expect none. Share your fire with a stranger tonight.
div.iching.hex.13.advice: The holdings are full and the road is clear. Trade what you carry before you reach the market; the price is good at the next halt.
div.iching.hex.14.advice: The mountain bows beneath heaven. Cross the high ground by the lower pass, and let the guides name the way.
div.iching.hex.15.advice: Thunder rises out of earth, and readiness is its own reward. Rise early and prepare for news at the second post.
div.iching.hex.16.advice: The cart follows the ruts that came before. Do not strike a new trail when the old road still holds water.
div.iching.hex.17.advice: The vessel is cracked but still carries water. Mend what you carry before setting out, even if it costs you a day.
div.iching.hex.18.advice: The marsh comes to the shore — approach the next city in company, not alone, for the guards watch the lone traveller harder.
div.iching.hex.19.advice: Look down from the tower before you descend to the gate. Watch the traffic for one watch before choosing your road.
div.iching.hex.2.advice: A beginning is tangled and heavy. Leave by the side gate and walk the smaller road; the main way is thick with carts this season.
div.iching.hex.20.advice: Bite through what resists you. Pay the gate toll without argument and keep your purse hidden until the city square.
div.iching.hex.21.advice: The ornament hides what lies beneath. Do not judge the road by the welcome; ask the market porters where the dust runs deep.
div.iching.hex.22.advice: The mountain crumbles. Travel light and do not trust the old bridge; take the ford instead, even if it costs a wet boot.
div.iching.hex.23.advice: What returns after winter is stronger than what stayed. A road closed last season may open again; ask at the station again.
div.iching.hex.24.advice: No false thread holds this weave. Trust the directions you received; do not listen to shortcuts told at the wine stall.
div.iching.hex.25.advice: The mountain holds great stores. Stock your bags here, for the next three stations keep poor markets.
div.iching.hex.26.advice: Nourish your company and your body. Spend a full day resting before the mountain crossing; thin travellers are stopped at the pass.
div.iching.hex.27.advice: The beam is too heavy for the house. Do not carry a full cargo on the desert road; split your goods or sell half.
div.iching.hex.28.advice: Water over water — the ford is deeper than it looks. Wait for a local boatman; do not cross alone.
div.iching.hex.29.advice: Fire holds to what feeds it. Attach yourself to a caravan even if it costs you coin; a lone flame draws bandits.
div.iching.hex.3.advice: A spring under a mountain runs blind. Ask the herders, not the merchants, which path the goats take to water.
div.iching.hex.30.advice: Influence draws like to like. Speak gently at the next toll house, and the guard may know which innkeepers trade in maps.
div.iching.hex.31.advice: Thunder and wind endure together. Choose the road that keeps the river in sight; do not turn inland for a rumour.
div.iching.hex.32.advice: The wise man retreats to higher ground before the flood. Skip the next river town and climb to the hill station.
div.iching.hex.33.advice: Great strength moves the cart through mud. Take the lowland marsh road while the dry season holds; do not delay.
div.iching.hex.34.advice: The sun advances over the plain — ride or walk while the light is full. Do not begin a stage in the last hour of day.
div.iching.hex.35.advice: Light is wounded but not extinguished. Travel the coast road at night under the moon; avoid midday heat on this stage.
div.iching.hex.36.advice: The household feeds itself before the road. Settle your accounts at this city before you take a single step out.
div.iching.hex.37.advice: Two faces look opposite ways. Your map and your guide disagree; stand still half a day and ask a third voice.
div.iching.hex.38.advice: The mountain blocks the water. Turn back at the landslide, even if you lose a day; the goat track is not a road.
div.iching.hex.39.advice: Thunder loosens the rain at last. The blocked road will open after the storm; wait in the caravanserai and bargain for provisions.
div.iching.hex.4.advice: Wait one more day. The ford is swollen with meltwater; a boat will come with the morning barge.
div.iching.hex.40.advice: Decrease opens the jar for pouring. Give a little of your cargo as gifts at the pass, and the guards will wave you through.
div.iching.hex.41.advice: Increase lifts the vessel higher. Accept a travelling companion who knows the language of the next province.
div.iching.hex.42.advice: Resolution parts the flooding waters. Choose now: the mountain road or the sea lane; drifting between them loses both.
div.iching.hex.43.advice: Encounter favours the first meeting. Approach the next city when the gate opens, not after the midday market thins, for the first buyer learns most.
div.iching.hex.44.advice: The marsh gathers streams into one pool. Gather news from three sources before you commit to a route across the steppe.
div.iching.hex.45.advice: The tree climbs the southern slope. Take the ascending ridge road, not the valley path; the melt has swollen the low streams.
div.iching.hex.46.advice: Confinement is a wall with a gate you have not yet tried. The main road is closed; ask the temple keeper about the pilgrim way.
div.iching.hex.47.advice: The well water is clear but the rope is short. Your coin is enough for the journey but not enough for haste; travel slowly.
div.iching.hex.48.advice: The hide is stripped — revolution remakes the old shape. Do not travel by the trade route this season; try the pilgrim road.
div.iching.hex.49.advice: The cauldron holds what feeds the village. Cook your own food on the road, even when the inn promises a hot meal.
div.iching.hex.5.advice: A dispute at the gate wastes daylight. Pay the claimed toll without raising your voice; the road beyond is worth more than the copper.
div.iching.hex.50.advice: A hundred li away, thunder rolls. Word will reach the next city before you do; arrive quietly and listen before you speak.
div.iching.hex.51.advice: Two mountains — stillness doubled at the pass. Do not cross the col today; the wind is turning and the cloud is low.
div.iching.hex.52.advice: The wild goose walks into the marsh one step at a time. Take the journey by short stages, resting at every well.
div.iching.hex.53.advice: The maiden joins the new house, and all alters. Your known maps end here; hire a local guide, not a merchant from the last city.
div.iching.hex.54.advice: Thunder and lightning fill the sky with abundance. The road buzzes with news and caravans; join a large company and keep your own pace.
div.iching.hex.55.advice: The traveller's fire must be small and quick. Sleep in a different inn each night; do not let any town grow accustomed to your face.
div.iching.hex.56.advice: The wind bends the reeds without breaking them. Adapt your route when the road is blocked; do not force a passage through closed country.
div.iching.hex.57.advice: The marsh mirrors the sky, and joy comes to those who rest. Pause a full day at the lake town and let the mules drink deep.
