market.zayton.item.cinnabar: Cinnabar from the mountain mines of the south, sold in both the raw stone and the ground powder — the latter in small stoppered bottles because the wind off the haven will carry it away by the grain.
market.zayton.item.dehua-porcelain: Blanc de Chine out of the Dehua kilns — unglazed on the surface, warm as ivory. The Arab merchants call it 'the fat of the earth' and pay the forty-four in the hundred freight without complaint.
market.zayton.item.ginger: Preserved ginger in clay jars sealed with wax, bound for the galleys of Hormuz and Aden. The spice merchants say a ship without ginger is a ship that will lose half its crew to the flux.
market.zayton.item.hangzhou-fan: Folding fans from Kinsay, their ribs of sandalwood, their leaves painted with calligraphy. A merchant who buys a crate of these at Zayton can sell them in Damascus for ten times the price.
market.zayton.item.lacquerware: Black and cinnabar-red lacquer from the workshops of Fuju, cured in the damp heat of the coastal summer. The Indian merchants prize it for the way candlelight moves across the surface like oil on dark water.
market.zayton.item.musk: The musk-pod from the deer of the Tibetan marches, brought down to Zayton by caravan through the passes. A single pod, no bigger than a walnut, will scent a cargo of silk for a month.
market.zayton.item.paper-money: The Kaan's own currency, printed on mulberry-bark sheets with the imperial seal in vermilion. The quay-side money-changers will swap silver for paper at a rate that changes with the tide.
market.zayton.item.porcelain: The white ware of Jingdezhen, packed in straw and sawdust, carried down the rivers on flat-bottomed boats. A percentage of every crate is broken in transit, and the merchants have already figured that cost into the price you pay.
market.zayton.item.rhubarb: The dried root of the Tangut rhubarb — worth more pound for pound than cinnamon in the apothecaries of Venice. The warehousemen weigh it on the same brass scales they use for pearls.
market.zayton.item.silk: Bales of raw Manzi silk, stacked eight-high in the customs shed, waiting to be weighed and taxed. The Kaan's clerks nick a corner of every bale to check the grade; finer than any the Persians spin.
market.zayton.item.sugar: Cane sugar from the plantations of Fuju, shipped up the coast in cone-shaped loaves wrapped in palm-leaf. A cone of sugar is the universal gift at the quay; no deal is closed without one.
market.zayton.item.tea: Tea pressed into bricks and stamped with the producer's chop. The quayside merchants will trade a brick for a sack of pepper straight across, and both sides consider it a bargain.
npc.npc-kiovia-mentor.name: The Rune-Carver of Kiovia
npc.npc-kiovia-mentor.omen: He cuts marks into birch before every ford.
npc.npc-zayton-mentor.name: The Woman Who Reads the Slips
npc.npc-zayton-mentor.omen: She has read slips for forty years, and remembers every master who ignored one.
retainer.cambaluc-mentor.fate_0: This year, a former student now high in the Kaan's service will offer him a pardon. Accepting means returning to Cambaluc — the one city he has sworn never to enter again.
retainer.cambaluc-mentor.fate_1: The scholar's eyes are failing. By the end of the year, he will need a scribe to read him the oracle books.
retainer.cambaluc-mentor.name: Scholar Wang of the Hanlin
retainer.cambaluc-mentor.origin: A Hanlin academician who fell from favour at the Kaan's court after disputing the interpretation of an oracle. He now teaches the I Ching to anyone who will listen.
retainer.cambaluc-mentor.quest: Wang believes that the true text of the I Ching was lost when the Qin emperor burned the books, and that a fragment survives in a monastery in the Tangut mountains. He seeks a travelling companion to help him find it.
retainer.cambaluc-mentor.sign: His fingernails are stained black from years of grinding ink. He has not written a single character since the day he left the court.
retainer.camel-driver.fate_0: This year, Bekter will attempt his forty-first crossing. The desert is a jealous wife, he says; she does not like to let a man go.
retainer.camel-driver.fate_1: One of Bekter's camels has developed a strange white patch on its flank. The old man believes it is a mark of blessing, but the other drivers call it a curse.
retainer.camel-driver.name: Old Bekter
retainer.camel-driver.origin: A Bactrian camel-driver who has crossed the Great Desert forty times. He has more miles on his knees than most men have in their whole bodies. He speaks to his camels in a language only they understand.
retainer.camel-driver.quest: Bekter once buried a hoard of silver at a place in the desert whose location he can only find by the stars. He wants to retrieve it before he dies. He will need help carrying it out.
retainer.camel-driver.sign: He can taste the water in the air. When he says a well is dry, every man in the caravan believes him — he has never been wrong.
retainer.cotanese-weaver.fate_0: A carpet Gulbibi wove ten years ago has been recognised by a merchant in Cambaluc as the work of a 'master of Khotan.' Buyers are searching for her. Fame will find her this year — whether she wants it or not.
retainer.cotanese-weaver.fate_1: The indigo crop failed this year. Her blue thread is running out, and without it, her carpets cannot be sold as the finest grade.
retainer.cotanese-weaver.name: Gulbibi the Weaver
retainer.cotanese-weaver.origin: A master carpet-weaver from Khotan, who can draw from memory the pattern of any carpet she has seen for more than five minutes. Her hands are stained with madder, indigo, and walnut.
retainer.cotanese-weaver.quest: Gulbibi's mother taught her a pattern that no other weaver in Khotan knows — a prayer for safe journey encoded in knot-counts and colour sequences. She wants to weave one last copy of it before her eyes fail.
retainer.cotanese-weaver.sign: She ties one knot in every carpet wrong, deliberately. 'Only God makes things perfect,' she says.
retainer.guard-aleppo.fate_0: A scar on his shoulder aches before storms. This year, it will ache for three weeks straight — and the storm that follows will change everything.
retainer.guard-aleppo.fate_1: An old comrade from the Mamluk corps has become a bandit chief in the mountains of Anatolia. Yusuf will have to choose: join him, turn him in, or pretend he never heard the name.
retainer.guard-aleppo.name: Yusuf the Circassian
retainer.guard-aleppo.origin: A former Mamluk slave-soldier who bought his freedom in the markets of Aleppo. He fought in the Sultan's cavalry against the Franks and the Mongols.
retainer.guard-aleppo.quest: Yusuf seeks the man who taught him to fight — an old weapons-master who retired to a monastery in the Caucasus. He wants to return the broken sword and receive a new one.
retainer.guard-aleppo.sign: He carries a sword with a broken tip. The break, he says, was a mercy; the man it broke against lived.
retainer.kinsay-mentor.fate_0: This year, a client whose fortune she once read will return — not for another reading, but for her. He has been looking for twenty years.
retainer.kinsay-mentor.fate_1: Lin's chart shows a clash between her fire and the year's water. The southern sea roads are dangerous for her this year; the northern roads, however, will bring an unexpected inheritance.
retainer.kinsay-mentor.name: Lin Sanniang
retainer.kinsay-mentor.origin: A fortune-teller from the pleasure quarters of Kinsay, who read a hundred faces a day and never forgot one. She learned the Four Pillars from an old astrologer who took her in as a girl.
retainer.kinsay-mentor.quest: Lin's mentor died leaving a sealed box that can only be opened on the day her chart predicts. She carries it everywhere but has never opened it. The predicted day falls this year — somewhere on the road.
retainer.kinsay-mentor.sign: She never reads her own chart. 'The gods do not need to know I am watching back,' she says.
retainer.mazu-priestess.fate_0: A ship blessed by A-Mei three years ago has been sighted off the coast of Champa. Everyone aboard was given up for dead. Their return will be either a miracle or a scandal.
retainer.mazu-priestess.fate_1: The temple of Mazu needs a new roof. A-Mei must raise the funds this year, or the spring rains will ruin the goddess's image.
retainer.mazu-priestess.name: A-Mei of the Sea
retainer.mazu-priestess.origin: A priestess of Mazu at the great temple in Zayton. She has blessed a thousand ships and watched a hundred of them fail to return. Her eyes are old with the sea.
retainer.mazu-priestess.quest: A-Mei believes that Mazu's power is fading because the source of her blessing — a sacred spring on the island of Meizhou — has been polluted by a shipwreck. She seeks travellers to help her cleanse it.
retainer.mazu-priestess.sign: The incense she burns in the temple always drifts toward the sea, never toward the land. She says Mazu is calling.
retainer.nestorian-priest.fate_0: This year, Father Simeon will find what he has been looking for — but it will not be what he expected. The Prester John of legend is dead; only his descendants remain, ruling a small tribe in the Ordos.
retainer.nestorian-priest.fate_1: A Nestorian bishop in Cambaluc has accused Simeon of heresy. The road east may be closed to him this year.
retainer.nestorian-priest.name: Father Simeon
retainer.nestorian-priest.origin: A Nestorian priest from Mosul, travelling east in search of the Christian kingdom of Prester John. He has crossed the steppe twice and been turned back twice.
retainer.nestorian-priest.quest: Simeon believes that the Nestorian church in Cambaluc holds a Gospel written in the hand of St. Thomas himself. He wants to see it, touch it, and copy it before he dies.
retainer.nestorian-priest.sign: He carries a reliquary that contains, he says, a fragment of the True Cross. No one has ever seen him open it.
retainer.steppe-guide.fate_0: This year, a blizzard will test him as no blizzard has before. If he survives it, his confidence will carry the whole party.
retainer.steppe-guide.fate_1: Temur's clan will call him home this year for a marriage he cannot refuse. He may return — or he may not.
retainer.steppe-guide.name: Temur the Herder
retainer.steppe-guide.origin: A Mongol of the Keraite clan, raised on the steppe north of the Gobi. He can navigate by the stars, read the weather in the taste of the wind, and find water where no man sees any.
retainer.steppe-guide.quest: Temur's elder brother was taken by a rival clan in a raid ten years ago. He has heard a rumour that the man is alive, a slave in the markets of Samarcand. He will not ask for help, but his eyes search every face in every crowd.
retainer.steppe-guide.sign: He cannot enter a walled city without first circling its walls three times. An old steppe custom, he says.
retainer.tartar-messenger.fate_0: A message Altan is carrying this year contains news that will start a war. He does not know it yet — but if he reads it, he will have to decide whether to deliver it.
retainer.tartar-messenger.fate_1: The Kaan's post is expanding this year. A new station will open in a place where no messenger has gone before. Altan will be the first — or someone else will.
retainer.tartar-messenger.name: Altan the Arrow
retainer.tartar-messenger.origin: A Tartar courier of the Kaan's yam, the imperial post. He can ride two hundred miles in a day, changing horses at every station. He knows every post-house between Cambaluc and Samarcand.
retainer.tartar-messenger.quest: Altan's father was a courier who died carrying a message from the Kaan to the Ilkhan. The message was never delivered. Altan wants to find out what it said and whether it changed the course of a war.
retainer.tartar-messenger.sign: He never dismounts on the left side of a horse. The one time he did, the horse threw him and he broke three ribs.
retainer.tauris-merchant.fate_0: This year, a debt from his past will find him. Pay it or flee — either way, the road changes.
retainer.tauris-merchant.fate_1: Mirza's network of informants will bring word of a caravan that doubles its value by the time it reaches the sea.
retainer.tauris-merchant.name: Mirza of Tabriz
retainer.tauris-merchant.origin: A Persian merchant who once ran the Genoese fondaco in Tauris. He knows every language between Venice and Cambaluc, and the price of every goods.
retainer.tauris-merchant.quest: Mirza owes a sum of silver to a merchant-house in Hormuz. He will not speak of it, but he watches every ship that docks in every port. Help him settle the debt, and he will share his knowledge of the southern sea roads.
retainer.tauris-merchant.sign: He never sleeps with his back to a door. When asked why, he changes the subject.
retainer.venetian-clerk.fate_0: Pietro's gambling debt will catch up with him this year. A Venetian agent in Tauris has a warrant — or says he does.
retainer.venetian-clerk.fate_1: A merchant in Kinsay has noticed Pietro's handwriting and offered him a position keeping the books of a pepper fleet. The salary is a fortune; the temptation to embezzle is greater.
retainer.venetian-clerk.name: Pietro the Clerk
retainer.venetian-clerk.origin: A Venetian notary's apprentice who stowed away on a galley to escape a gambling debt. He has a beautiful hand for writing, a head for figures, and a complete inability to keep his mouth shut.
retainer.venetian-clerk.quest: Pietro wants to compose a book of his travels — a Merchants' Guide to the East, with prices, routes, and notes on every city. He needs to visit twelve more cities before he has enough material.
retainer.venetian-clerk.sign: He writes a letter to Venice every month and posts none of them. The stack in his saddlebag is a year thick.
retainer.zayton-mentor.fate_0: This year, the monsoon will arrive a week early. If he is at sea when it comes, his ship will outrun the storm. If he is in port, the harbour will be blocked for a month.
retainer.zayton-mentor.fate_1: A rival captain has challenged his monopoly on the Zayton-Hormuz route. Majid will need to prove his worth this year — or lose his ship.
retainer.zayton-mentor.name: Captain Majid of Zayton
retainer.zayton-mentor.origin: An Arab sea-captain who has made the voyage from Zayton to Hormuz thirty times. He knows every reef, every current, and every monsoon between the China Sea and the Persian Gulf.
retainer.zayton-mentor.quest: Twenty years ago, Majid lost a chest of pearls overboard in a storm off the coast of Champa. A diver recently claimed to have found it. Majid will detour a thousand miles on the rumour alone.
retainer.zayton-mentor.sign: He always consults the temple lots before setting sail. He has never ignored a lot in his life — and he has never been shipwrecked.
sticker.st-aden-shrine.body: You keep a little mark of the mandir of Aden, taken at the gate of the spice road. Aden is the haven where the ships of India come with their cargoes, and the people of the province adore Mahommet; yet the temple door stood open to a stranger who came with courtesy. You left as you entered, without asking price or promise, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you along the quay. The mark is small, but it stays with you, and it opens the way where no letter would.
sticker.st-aden-shrine.name: Aden Shrine
sticker.st-badashan-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the masjid of Badashan, the province whose kings trace their blood to King Alexander and the daughter of King Darius, and call themselves Zulcarniain in the Saracen tongue. The people worship Mahommet and speak a language of their own. In the mountains the balas rubies are dug from great caves under the earth, on the king's account alone; no one else dares dig in that mountain, on pain of forfeiture of life as well as goods. You visited the mosque, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The mark stays with you.
sticker.st-badashan-shrine.name: Badashan Shrine
sticker.st-balc-lapis.body: You keep a block of raw lapis lazuli from the mines of Badakhshan, twelve days east of Balc, bought in the great caravanserai — a fortress-sized courtyard ringed with stables for a thousand camels, its storerooms stacked with bales of silk and leather sacks of the blue stone. The lapis is sold in rough blocks and traded for silver, silk, and spices, and it is the city's chief treasure. The caravanserai never sleeps; fires burn in the arcades all night, and the smell of lamb kebab and saffron rice hangs in the air. You kept the block through those nights.
sticker.st-balc-lapis.name: A Block of Badakhshan Lapis
sticker.st-balc-magi.body: You keep the fire of the Magi, which they say has never been extinguished since the days of Zoroaster, a thousand years before the Prophet. They call the place the Tomb of the Magi, and say the three wise men who visited the infant Christ are buried here, in three stone sarcophagi that still bear traces of gold leaf. The Magi in their white robes chant the ancient hymns at dawn and dusk, and pilgrims from Persia, India, and distant Cathay leave offerings of incense and silver coins. The dream you dreamed there, you keep to yourself.
sticker.st-balc-magi.name: The Fire of the Magi
sticker.st-balc-ruby.body: You keep a balas ruby from the mountains of Balc, a stone worth a ship in Venice. It changed hands in the great caravanserai, where merchants of every nation keep their chambers and the storerooms are stacked with bales of silk and leather sacks of lapis from Badakhshan. The price it fetched would buy a vessel outright in Venice, and the merchants who weighed it knew its worth to a grain. You turn it in your palm when the road is long, and it still seems too small to be worth so much.
sticker.st-balc-ruby.name: A Balas Ruby
sticker.st-balc-ruins.body: You keep the memory of Bactra, the mother of cities, whose broken ramparts stand about Balc. Alexander took Roxana of Sogdiana to wife within these walls, when the city enclosed more ground than any in Asia and its temples held treasure from India, Persia, and Greece. Now the domes are collapsed and the palaces empty, and the new houses are smaller, built from the stones of the old. Yet the market is alive again, and lapis, rubies, and Turkoman horses keep the city's heart beating. You carried this away from the ruins, and it has not left you.
sticker.st-balc-ruins.name: The Ruins of Bactra
sticker.st-baldacum-brocade.body: You keep a length of Baudas brocade worked with gold, woven in the city where they make many silk stuffs and gold brocades — nasich, nac, and cramoisy — richly wrought with figures of beasts and birds. It came out of the covered markets of Baudas, where the silk-merchants keep one vaulted lane and the silversmiths another, and each guild maintains its own mosque, bathhouse, and coffee-house. The money-changers sit behind low tables covered with mountains of silver dirhams, and the merchants drink sherbet cooled with snow from the Kurdish mountains. You keep the gold thread, and the pattern of it.
sticker.st-baldacum-brocade.name: A Bolt of Baudas Silk
sticker.st-baldacum-fall.body: You keep the proof of the fall of Baudas, the story told in the bazaars. The Caliph, trusting in his gold and his twenty thousand guards, refused to pay tribute to the Great Khan. Hulagu marched with a host that blackened the plain from horizon to horizon, broke the dikes of the Tigris, and drained the Caliph's moat. When the walls fell, he shut the Caliph in his own treasury — a tower full of gold, silver, jewels, and silk — and told him to eat his treasure. The Caliph starved among his wealth, and the city burned for a month.
sticker.st-baldacum-fall.name: The Fall of the City of Baudas
sticker.st-baldacum-palace.body: You keep the emptiness of the Caliph's hall at Baudas, the great palace whose golden dome could be seen three days' journey away across the flat plain of the Tigris. Its halls were hung with silk embroidered with gold thread, its gardens watered by channels drawn from the river, and its treasury held the tribute of a hundred nations. The Caliph himself was never seen except by a handful of servants. When Hulagu came to the walls, all that gold and all those swords could not save him. The hall stands empty, and you carry the emptiness with you.
sticker.st-baldacum-palace.name: The Caliph's Empty Hall
sticker.st-cail-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the mandir of Cail, and your name carries a little more weight in the city for it. Cail is the great and noble city where the ships from Hormos, from Kis, from Aden, and from all Arabia touch, laden with horses and with other things for sale, and the King favours merchants and foreigners. A stranger is watched here, and a stranger who enters the temple with courtesy is spoken of. The small sign of the place stays with you, a good word laid up against the day of need.
sticker.st-cail-shrine.name: Cail Shrine
sticker.st-calatu-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the mandir of Calatu, the strong city on the gulf where the Melic of Hormos takes refuge in time of war. The people are Saracens subject to Hormos, and they grow no corn here but get it from abroad. The haven is large and good, frequented by ships with goods from India, and from this city the spices are distributed among the cities of the interior. You visited the temple, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-calatu-shrine.name: Calatu Shrine
sticker.st-camadi-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the masjid of Camadi, and your name carries a little more weight in the plain for it. Camadi was formerly a great and noble place, but now it is of little consequence, for the Tartars in their incursions have several times ravaged it. The plain is a very hot region, and the fruits of the country are dates, pistachioes, and apples of Paradise. The sign of the place stays with you, with the memory of how much a city may lose and still stand.
sticker.st-camadi-shrine.name: Camadi Shrine
sticker.st-cambaluc-court.body: You keep the great hall of the Kaan at Cambaluc, the largest roofed building in the world, where six thousand men can sit at table when the Kaan holds his feasts. The roof is painted vermilion, blue, green, and gold; dragons coil around the beams and phoenixes spread their wings across the ceiling. The walls are hung with silk embroidered with hunts on horseback and battles between elephants and tigers. The Kaan sits on a raised dais at the northern end, on a throne of carved jade, so that his gaze falls on every guest.
sticker.st-cambaluc-court.name: The Great Hall of the Kaan
sticker.st-cambaluc-hill.body: You keep the art of the green hill of Cambaluc, raised in the Kaan's great park of green jade, jasper, and lapis lazuli, brought block by block from the quarries of Badakhshan and Cotan. The trees upon it were dug up by the roots in distant forests, wrapped in silk and wet earth, and carried here on the backs of elephants; they grow as green as in their native soil. A thousand gardeners water them daily by hand, and the Kaan walks among them alone in the evenings, when no one may disturb him. You keep the hill.
sticker.st-cambaluc-hill.name: The Mountain of Green Jade
sticker.st-cambaluc-suburbs.body: You keep the counting of the twelve suburbs of Cambaluc, each larger than most cities of Christendom or Islam. The merchants of every province of the Kaan's empire — Cathay, Manzi, Tangut, Tibet, the Golden Horde, Persia, and India — keep their warehouses and counting-houses there; a thousand cart-loads of silk enter the city every day, and forty cart-loads of pepper and spice are consumed daily. No poor person goes hungry, for the Kaan maintains public granaries that distribute rice and millet to anyone who asks. You counted the cart-loads with the tally-men, and you keep the sum of it.
sticker.st-cambaluc-suburbs.name: The Twelve Suburbs of Cambaluc
sticker.st-campichu-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the sì of Campichu, the capital of Tangut, where the Idolaters keep an enormous number of idols in their minsters and abbeys. Some of the idols are a good ten paces in stature, of wood, clay, or stone, all highly polished and covered with gold; the great ones lie at length, with figures round about as if adoring before them. Religious recluses among the people lead a more virtuous life than the rest. You visited the monastery, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-campichu-shrine.name: Campichu Shrine
sticker.st-camul-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the masjid of Camul, the first oasis east of the Great Desert, where the traveler who has survived the sand begins to breathe again. The people are Idolaters; they once practiced a strange custom of offering their wives to passing strangers as a mark of hospitality, until the Great Khan forbade it, though the old people still speak of it. You visited the mosque, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The melons of this district are the sweetest on the whole road, and the little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-camul-shrine.name: Camul Shrine
sticker.st-cascar-carpet.body: You keep a carpet of Cascar, woven so fine that a man can pass it through a finger-ring. The women worked for months on it, knowing every dye by its smell: madder-root for red, indigo for blue, pomegranate rind for yellow, walnut hull for brown, and a secret mineral for a green that fades only after a hundred years. The patterns are said to contain prayers, protecting the owner from the evil eye, from snake-bite, and from the spirits of the desert. A merchant who buys a Cascar carpet never travels without it, and neither do you.
sticker.st-cascar-carpet.name: A Cascar Carpet
sticker.st-cascar-garden.body: You keep the garden of the Tarim, the richest oasis on the Silk Road, where the melt-water from the Pamir and the Karakorum feeds a green paradise in the desert. Orchards of apricot, pomegranate, mulberry, walnut, and almond stretch for miles along the irrigation canals, and the vines grow so heavy with grapes that the trellises must be replaced every year. The people worship Mahommet and keep many old customs from before the time of the Prophet. You tasted the melons of Cascar — the sweetest and largest in the world — and have spoken of nothing else since.
sticker.st-cascar-garden.name: The Garden of the Tarim
sticker.st-cascar-sleepers.body: You keep the cave of the Seven Sleepers, cut in a limestone cliff outside Cascar, where seven holy men are said to sleep. The Muslims say they have slept since before the time of the Prophet, waiting for the Day of Judgment; the Christians say they are their own Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, miraculously transported here. A mosque and a chapel stand side by side at the cave entrance, and the monks and the mullahs take turns sweeping the cave, the offerings of candles, incense, and silver coins divided equally. You carried away both names of the sleepers.
sticker.st-cascar-sleepers.name: The Cave of the Seven Sleepers
sticker.st-chamba-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the masjid of Chamba, the rich country reached by sailing west-south-west from Zayton for fifteen hundred miles. The people are Idolaters and pay the Great Kaan a yearly tribute of elephants and nothing but elephants, ever since his Baron Sagatu came with a great force of horse and foot against their aged king, who saw the havoc and sent messengers to make his peace. You visited the mosque, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The little mark stays with you, a quiet name in a land that ransomed itself with elephants.
sticker.st-chamba-shrine.name: Chamba Shrine
sticker.st-chandu-mares.body: You keep the sacred white mares of Chandu, the herd of a thousand that are not ridden or worked, but milked twice a day in golden vessels for the Kaan's table; no one of lesser rank may taste it. The monks of the Palace of the Spring tend them in the meadow at the park's northern end. Once a year, at the great Mongol festival, the Kaan pours the milk on the ground as an offering to the spirits of the Eternal Blue Sky and the Golden Earth. No foreigner has ever witnessed this ceremony.
sticker.st-chandu-mares.name: The Sacred White Mares
sticker.st-chandu-palace.body: You keep the gilded cane palace of Chandu, the summer palace of the Great Kaan, built entirely of cane — the columns, the walls, everything. The cane is harvested from a forest in the south of Manzi, split, lacquered, gilded with gold leaf, and lashed together with silken cords, so it can be taken down and moved when the Kaan travels. Dragons in green, blue, vermilion, and gold coil up every pillar, and the marble floors are so polished they reflect the gilded ceiling. No other building is so light and yet so splendid. You keep it as it stood.
sticker.st-chandu-palace.name: The Gilded Cane Palace
sticker.st-chandu-park.body: You keep the Kaan's game park at Chandu, enclosed by a wall that runs for sixteen miles, with a forest so dense that a man on horseback cannot cross it in a single day. It is stocked with deer, boar, wild ass, bear, and leopard, and a lake holds every species of waterfowl known to man. The Kaan rides here with his falconers, huntsmen, and cheetah-keepers, and you watched his gerfalcons fed in their mews. In one corner the thousand white mares are kept, so sacred that no one of lower rank may ride them, touch them, or walk in their pasture.
sticker.st-chandu-park.name: The Kaan's Game Park
sticker.st-chinangli-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the sì of Chinangli, and your name carries a little more weight there now. The city belongs to the Great Kaan and stands on a great and wide river, on which a large traffic in silk goods and spices passes up and down; the people are Idolaters and have paper-money. Five days south, the towns burn their dead and live by trade and handicrafts, in great abundance. The sign of the place stays with you, and with it the memory of a great river busy with silk and spices.
sticker.st-chinangli-shrine.name: Chinangli Shrine
sticker.st-cotan-buddha.body: You keep the dust of the buried city on the old river terrace beyond Cotan, where the water no longer flows. The sand has buried an older city — a thousand monasteries, a hundred stupas, and painted caves beyond counting. The wind uncovers fragments each day: a painted face of a bodhisattva with kohl-rimmed eyes, a hand raised in blessing, lotus petals in gold and vermilion. The old people drink this dust as medicine, and the desert reclaims whatever the expeditions of Cambaluc uncover. You keep the dust, and the names of the buried monasteries.
sticker.st-cotan-buddha.name: The Buddha Dust
sticker.st-cotan-jade.body: You keep a piece of Cotan jade — white like congealed mutton-fat, green like the first leaves of spring. It comes from the two rivers that carry the stones down from the mountains. In autumn, when the rivers run low, the men wade into the cold water and feel for the stones with their bare feet, diving to bring them up. The largest stones go to the Kaan's agents, to be carved in Cambaluc into cups, bracelets, and belt-buckles, and a fine piece is worth its weight in gold. You keep a piece of it.
sticker.st-cotan-jade.name: A Piece of Cotan Jade
sticker.st-cotan-rivers.body: You keep the reading of the rivers above Cotan, where the jade comes down from the mountains — white jade like congealed mutton-fat, and green jade like the first leaves of spring. In autumn, when the rivers run low, the men of Cotan wade into the cold water and feel for the stones with their bare feet; when they find one, they dive and bring it up. The divers read the water — its depth, its season, its gravel — as other men read a page. You learned that reading from them, and you keep it.
sticker.st-cotan-rivers.name: The Jade Rivers
sticker.st-cotan-silk.body: You keep a bolt of Cotan silk, spun finer than any in Cathay — a single thread, finer than a human hair, can run for a thousand paces without breaking. The country round is all mulberry trees, and the silk is dyed with saffron for yellow, indigo for blue, madder for red, and cochineal for crimson. At the looms, two women pass the shuttle back and forth while singing a song that keeps the rhythm. A bolt large enough for a robe sells for its weight in silver in Cambaluc's bazaars. You keep the bolt, and the song with it.
sticker.st-cotan-silk.name: A Bolt of Cotan Silk
sticker.st-esher-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the mandir of Esher, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Esher lies four hundred miles from the Port of Aden, under a king who is subject to the Soldan; the people are Saracens, and the haven is very good, with ships from India coming and chargers going out. White incense grows in this country, and no one dares sell it but the Prince, who takes it from the people at ten livres the hundredweight and sells it at sixty. The small sign of the place stays with you.
sticker.st-esher-shrine.name: Esher Shrine
sticker.st-kenjanfu-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the sì of Kenjanfu, the capital of a kingdom that in old times was noble, rich, and powerful, and is now held by Mangalai, son of the Great Kaan, who hath crowned him king thereof. The country round is planted with mulberries, on the leaves of which the silkworms feed, and there is plenty of game of all sorts, both of beasts and birds. You visited the monastery, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you through the city of great trade and industry. The little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-kenjanfu-shrine.name: Kenjanfu Shrine
sticker.st-kerman-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the masjid of Kerman, the kingdom of Persia where the turquoises are found in great abundance in the mountains, and where the best falcons in the world are found. The people are very skilful in making harness of war — saddles, bridles, spurs, swords, bows, and quivers — and the ladies of the country work silk embroidery with figures of beasts and birds, trees and flowers, so deftly that their hangings are marvels to see. You visited the mosque, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-kerman-shrine.name: Kerman Shrine
sticker.st-keshimur-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the masjid of Keshimur, the province men say is the very source from which Idolatry spread abroad. The people are Idolaters, with a language of their own, and they have an astonishing acquaintance with enchantment: they make their idols to speak, and by their sorceries bring changes of weather and darkness. The clime is finely tempered, neither very hot nor very cold, and the strong passes let the country keep its independence. You visited the mosque, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The mark stays with you.
sticker.st-keshimur-shrine.name: Keshimur Shrine
sticker.st-kinsay-canals.body: You keep the twelve thousand bridges of Kinsay, the city built on water, where the streets are canals and the boats are the carriages. The bridges are of stone, and so tall that a ship with its mast raised can pass beneath without lowering the yard. A man could spend his whole life in Kinsay and never walk more than a hundred paces on dry land. From the drum-tower, a hundred canals radiate, their embankments straight as a sword-cut. The city has no walls — the water is its wall, guarded by the Kaan's fleet of patrol boats.
sticker.st-kinsay-canals.name: The Twelve Thousand Bridges
sticker.st-kinsay-lake.body: You keep the West Lake of Kinsay as it stood by moonlight, when the lanterns hung from the awning poles. The pleasure boats float day and night, painted in gold, blue, and vermilion — each boat a floating pavilion, with musicians playing the pipa and the guqin, and dancers in costumes embroidered with phoenixes. The lake is so large that a circuit takes a whole day, and its islands hold pleasure-palaces. A man who has not seen the West Lake by moonlight has not seen the most beautiful thing in the Kaan's empire.
sticker.st-kinsay-lake.name: The West Lake by Moonlight
sticker.st-kinsay-markets.body: You keep the account of the ten great markets of Kinsay, each one half a mile on a side, surrounded by double-storied warehouses. Every fish of sea and lake, every fruit of the earth, every fabric, spice, drug, and perfume is sold in one of the ten squares, and forty cart-loads of pepper pass the customs every day. The main street is so finely paved that no water stands on it. On either side are bathhouses and restaurants, where a man bathes in perfumed water and dines on ten courses for a few copper coins.
sticker.st-kinsay-markets.name: The Ten Great Markets of Kinsay
sticker.st-lop-jade.body: You keep the jade of Lop, bought from the dealer who spreads his stones on black velvet. In a low voice he told you where the jade comes from: the riverbeds above Cotan, where the streams run down from the snow mountains and lay their gravel bare when the autumn waters fall, so that one who knows the season buys at the source for a tenth of the price. A piece of mutton-fat white jade the size of a man's fist costs more than a camel, and light passes through it like water. You keep his word with the stone.
sticker.st-lop-jade.name: Lop Jade
sticker.st-melibar-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the mandir of Melibar, the great kingdom towards the west whose people are Idolaters, with a language and a king of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. From this kingdom and from Gozurat more than a hundred corsair vessels go forth every year, joining in fleets of twenty or thirty that cover some hundred miles of sea, signalling one to another by fire or smoke, so that no merchant ship can escape them. You visited the temple, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-melibar-shrine.name: Melibar Shrine
sticker.st-ormus-fort.body: You keep the fortress of Hormos, guarding the strait where the Persian Gulf opens into the Sea of India. Its walls of sun-baked brick and coral stone are thick enough to turn any mangonel, and its cisterns hold enough water to withstand a year's siege. Every ship that enters the harbor pays its toll in pepper and silk; the customs officer sits in a shaded alcove by the quay, weighing every bale on a brass scale. The city lives on the sea — every man is a sailor, a pearl-diver, or a merchant. You stood there, and you keep it.
sticker.st-ormus-fort.name: The Harbor Fort of Hormos
sticker.st-ormus-spice.body: You keep the first spice from the Indies bought at Hormos, where pepper, cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, cloves, and cardamom arrive on Arab dhows and Chinese junks. The warehouses are stacked with sacks marked in seven scripts, and the heat is so great a candle left inside will melt; men work at dawn and sleep through the midday. A cargo of pepper bought here for ten thousand bezants sells for sixty thousand in Venice, and the merchant princes' houses have wind-towers that funnel the sea breeze into cool underground chambers. You keep the spice, and the smell of the monsoon.
sticker.st-ormus-spice.name: Spices from the Indies
sticker.st-ormus-wind.body: You keep the warning of the Wind of Death at Hormos, so hot that men caught in the open drop dead where they stand. The houses are built with tall towers that catch the slightest breeze and funnel it down into underground chambers; on the worst days the whole population sits in the irrigation channels up to their chins — men, women, animals together — and the dead are buried at night. A merchant who plans his arrival for the summer finds the city half-deserted, the warehouses shuttered, and the harbor empty of ships. You keep the warning.
sticker.st-ormus-wind.name: The Wind of Death
sticker.st-sachiu.body: You carry away a small sign of Sachiu, the city on the edge of the Great Desert, reached after thirty days of crossing, in the province of Tangut. The people are Idolaters, with a peculiar language; they are no traders, but live by the fruits of the earth, and their many abbeys and minsters are full of idols of divers fashions, to which they pay great honour. Here the caravans restock after the terrible crossing, and the irrigated fields grow excellent melons and wheat. You set what you saw into your travel book, and the sign stays with you.
sticker.st-sachiu.name: Sachiu
sticker.st-saianfu-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the sì of Saianfu, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Saianfu is a very great and noble city, ruling over twelve other large and rich cities, and is itself a seat of great trade and manufacture, with much silk, from which they weave fine stuffs. It held out against the Great Kaan for three years after the rest of Manzi had surrendered, for the great and deep waters round about it let his troops approach from the north side only. The sign of the place stays with you.
sticker.st-saianfu-shrine.name: Saianfu Shrine
sticker.st-samarcanda-dome.body: You keep a place beneath the turquoise dome of the Gur-i-Mir, rising above the old city like a second sky. Samarcand is called the garden of the world: its streets are lined with canals shaded by plane trees, every courtyard has a fountain, every mosque a turquoise dome, and the Registan's three great madrasas are the heart of learning in Central Asia, where scholars come from every country of Islam to study law, theology, astronomy, and medicine. Between Baghdad and Cambaluc there is no city whose name carries more weight with the caravans.
sticker.st-samarcanda-dome.name: Beneath the Turquoise Dome
sticker.st-samarcanda-gardens.body: You keep the walk of the canals of Samarcand, the city they call the garden of the world. Its streets are lined with canals shaded by plane trees, and every courtyard has a fountain, every mosque a turquoise dome. The Registan square, with its three great madrasas, is the heart of learning in Central Asia; scholars come from every country of Islam to study law, theology, astronomy, and medicine under the blue-tiled arches. Between Baghdad and Cambaluc there is no city richer, no city more beautiful. You walked its canals, and you keep the green of them.
sticker.st-samarcanda-gardens.name: The Garden of the World
sticker.st-samarcanda-paper.body: You keep a sheaf of Samarcand paper, the best in the world, beaten and polished smooth with stone until it shines like watered silk. The secret was learned from Chinese prisoners taken in battle, when the armies of Islam first crossed the Oxus, but they have surpassed their teachers — the paper is whiter, smoother, and more durable than any made in Cathay. A single sheet can cost a day's wages for a skilled worker, but the calligraphers say it is worth it: ink never bleeds on Samarcand paper, and a book written on it will last three hundred years.
sticker.st-samarcanda-paper.name: Samarcand Paper
sticker.st-samarcanda-stone.body: You keep the mark of the weeping stone of Samarcand, the pillar of black basalt in the courtyard of the great mosque, brought here, they say, by the Prophet himself. It is polished by centuries of hands touching it for blessing. They say the stone weeps before disaster — drops of water appear on its surface, and within a year war, plague, or earthquake strikes the city. The last time it wept was the year before the Mongol rider first appeared on the northern horizon. You pressed your forehead to it, and the mark stays with you.
sticker.st-samarcanda-stone.name: The Weeping Stone
sticker.st-siju-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the sì of Siju, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Siju is a great, rich, and noble city, flourishing with trade and manufactures; the people are Idolaters, burn their dead, use paper-money, and are subjects of the Great Kaan, and their extensive and fertile plains produce abundance of wheat and other grain. Three days south the great river Caramoran flows down from Prester John's country. The sign of the place stays with you.
sticker.st-siju-shrine.name: Siju Shrine
sticker.st-sinju-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the sì of Sinju, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Sinju is a city of no great size, but it possesses a very great amount of shipping and trade, for it stands on the greatest river in the world — the Kian — which is in some places ten miles wide, in others eight, in others six, and more than a hundred days' journey in length. On its waters merchandize is perpetually coming and going, enriching the city. The sign of the place stays with you.
sticker.st-sinju-shrine.name: Sinju Shrine
sticker.st-suju-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the sì of Suju, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Suju is a very great and noble city of some sixty miles in circuit, whose people are accomplished traders and most skilful craftsmen, making gold brocade and other stuffs from their great quantity of silk; there are also many philosophers and leeches. The city has six thousand bridges, all of stone, and so lofty that a galley, or even two galleys at once, could pass underneath one of them. The sign of the place stays with you.
sticker.st-suju-shrine.name: Suju Shrine
sticker.st-taican-shrine.body: You keep the mark of the masjid of Taican, the fortified place with a great corn market, where the mountains are all composed of salt. It is the best in the world, so hard that it can only be broken with iron picks, and so abundant that it would supply the whole world to the end of time; people from all the countries round, to some thirty days' journey, come to fetch it. Other mountains grow almonds and pistachioes, exceedingly cheap. You visited the mosque, and word of your conduct ran ahead of you. The little mark stays with you.
sticker.st-taican-shrine.name: Taican Shrine
sticker.st-tanpiju-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the sì of Tanpiju, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Tanpiju is a great, rich, and fine city under Kinsay, a day's journey to the south-east through a plenteous region of dwellings and charming gardens. The people are subject to the Kaan, have paper-money, and are Idolaters who burn their dead; they live by trade and manufactures and handicrafts, and have all necessaries in great plenty and cheapness. The sign of the place stays with you, and with it the memory of the gardens that line the road.
sticker.st-tanpiju-shrine.name: Tanpiju Shrine
sticker.st-tauris-gardens.body: You keep the gardens of Tauris, stretching for miles along the qanats that bring water from the mountains. The great lords of the Ilkhanate — Persian viziers, Mongol noyans, Armenian merchants, and Turkish amirs — keep their summer pavilions here: open halls with tiled fountains, shaded by plane trees and cypress, surrounded by orchards of apricot, pomegranate, almond, and pistachio. The air smells of jasmine, rose, and watered earth, and the fruit is the finest in Persia. The gardeners say: a man who drinks the water of Tauris and eats its apricots will never want to leave.
sticker.st-tauris-gardens.name: The Gardens of Tauris
sticker.st-tauris-pearl.body: You keep a Tabriz pearl from the covered market of Tauris, where the Moslem traders sell silk from China and Cathay, pearls from the Gulf, and cloth of gold from Baghdad. It came to you at the toll-master's price, in a city where nearly every foreign merchant-house keeps an agent — the Genoese in their fortress-like fondaco near the Great Bazaar, the Armenians in their caravanserai by the east gate. Every bale that passes through the city pays a tax to the Ilkhan, and you paid yours. The pearl is small, the price was fair, and it stays with you.
sticker.st-tauris-pearl.name: A Tabriz Pearl
sticker.st-tauris-road-sense.body: You keep the road warning of Tauris, taken from the foreign merchants who do not merely name places. One points south toward Ctesiphon and marks the road in charcoal; another warns that the road to Baudas follows a different rhythm of tolls and water; and a third keeps a water ledger that gives you one more day's measure between wells. Their answers were useful only because you pressed them for the detail that belongs to your own journey — the tolls, the wells, the levy. You carry the warning with you, and the next departure is no longer blind.
sticker.st-tauris-road-sense.name: The Road Warning from Tauris
sticker.st-tauris-view.body: You keep the view from the Ilkhan's hill at Tauris, where the whole plain lies open — a green island in the brown Persian plateau, dotted with the smoke of a thousand cooking-fires. The city has outgrown every wall ever built around it, and its suburbs stretch for miles across the plain, a patchwork of orchards, workshops, gardens, and caravanserais, where Persian, Turkish, Armenian, Georgian, and Frankish merchants trade the goods of two continents. Below the palace, gardens of cypress and rose are watered by qanats that bring snow-melt from the mountains. You keep that view.
sticker.st-tauris-view.name: The Plain from the Ilkhan's Hill
sticker.st-tenduc-shrine.body: You carry away a small sign of the ovoo of Tenduc, the sacred cairn, and your name carries a little more weight there now. Tenduc is the province whose king, George by name, is of the lineage of Prester John and holds his land under the Great Kaan; the rule is in the hands of the Christians, though there are plenty of Idolaters and worshippers of Mahommet. Here is found the stone from which Azure is made, and fine camlets of different colours are woven from camel's hair. The sign of the sacred cairn stays with you.
sticker.st-tenduc-shrine.name: Tenduc Shrine
sticker.st-zayton-haven.body: You keep the haven of Zayton, where the quay is never quiet. Pepper comes in sacks the height of a man; pearls weighed in brass scales, lignaloes and sandalwood stacked like cordwood. The merchant pays dearly here: the Kaan takes a tamghā on everything, ten in the hundred, plus the ship's charge — thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on bulky, four and forty on pepper. Between the freight and the Kaan's due a man pays out a good half of his cargo's worth, yet on the other half the profit is so great that he is glad to come back with more.
sticker.st-zayton-haven.name: The Burnt Forest of Masts
sticker.st-zayton-mazu.body: You keep the smoke of the sea-temple of Zayton, above the anchorage, where no shipmaster of this coast puts out without going up to it first. They burn paper there, and set out a dish of rice and a cup of wine, and shake a bamboo cylinder of numbered slips until one falls; the slip is carried to an old woman by the door, who reads what is written against that number. The sailors do not call this fortune-telling. They call it asking. You stood at the back and watched, and you keep the asking with you.
sticker.st-zayton-mazu.name: Smoke at the Sea-Temple
sticker.st-zayton-silk.body: You keep a bolt of silk bought from a Manzi weaver in the foreign quarter of Zayton, where the merchants of India, of Persia, and of the Arab lands have their own houses of prayer, long enough that their grandsons are buried in this soil. Persian and Arabic and the local tongue are bargained in under one roof, and a man who has none will find his purse lighter than his understanding. Nobody in the quarter finds any of this remarkable, which is itself the most remarkable thing about it. You keep the silk, and the lesson.
sticker.st-zayton-silk.name: A Bolt of Manzi Silk

ui.boot.verse.libai.line_1: Far beyond the Jingmen gates, I come to travel from the land of Chu.
ui.boot.verse.libai.line_2: Mountains end where the plains begin; the river enters the boundless wild.

ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_1.line_1: A merchant has no settled home; wherever profit lies, he goes.
ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_1.line_2: At the gate he seeks companions; within, he bids his kin farewell.

ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_2.line_1: For pearls he sails the ocean; for jade he climbs Jing and Heng.
ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_2.line_2: North for Tangut horses, west for Tibetan parrots.
ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_2.source: Ballad of the Merchant · Tang dynasty · Yuan Zhen
ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_3.line_1: His business circles all beneath heaven, then brings him back to Chang'an.
ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_3.line_2: In the eastern and western markets, buyers come to greet him in turn.
ui.boot.verse.yuanzhen_3.source: Ballad of the Merchant · Tang dynasty · Yuan Zhen
ui.boot.verse.zhangji.line_1: Westward from Jinling the merchants are many, born aboard amid wind and waves.
ui.boot.verse.zhangji.line_2: Before sailing they draw near the river mouth and pour wine to the god at the prow.
